A BMJ Global Health study in October 2025 found its 640 grants worth about $5.5 billion in 2000–2024 went over 80% to infectious diseases and about 60% to polio, with under 1% for non-communicable diseases. The authors said WHO stays open to donor influence unless member states pay more.
orgs.cite: WHO contributor data; BMJ Global Health, 'Who's leading WHO? ... Gates Foundation's grants to WHO, 2000-2024', 28 October 2025 (BMJ Group release)

orgs.d: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) lends to countries in crisis on condition that they change their policies, and its staff move into the national posts that negotiate with it. Reza Baqir, an IMF staff member who had been its mission chief for Romania and Bulgaria, was appointed Governor of the State Bank of Pakistan on 4 May 2019, while Pakistan was negotiating an IMF bailout. A central bank governor sets interest rates and manages the currency, both points in such talks. Reuters reported he was appointed a day after his predecessor was abruptly removed. He served until May 2022.

The World Bank, an intergovernmental development lender created in 1944, has its own senior staff move into the national ministries that borrow from it and negotiate with it. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala spent 25 years at the Bank, which lends to Nigeria, and was a managing director from December 2007 to 2011. President Goodluck Jonathan then appointed her Nigeria's finance minister and coordinating minister for the economy on 17 August 2011, a post she held until May 2015, putting a Bank insider in charge of the borrower's side of the relationship. She became Director-General of the World Trade Organization in March 2021.

orgs.n: International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG)
orgs.d: The International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG) was set up by a 2006 UN–Guatemala agreement to help Guatemalan prosecutors take apart criminal networks inside the state; on this map it is the investigator, not the party reaching in. In 2015 CICIG and Guatemala's Public Ministry exposed 'La Línea', a bribery ring inside the customs service that reached Vice-President Roxana Baldetti and President Otto Pérez Molina. Congress lifted Pérez Molina's immunity 132–0 and he resigned on 2 September 2015; both were sentenced to 16 years in December 2022. CICIG helped break up over 70 networks before President Jimmy Morales shut it down in 2019.

orgs.n: Tony Blair Institute for Global Change
orgs.d: The Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, a non-profit founded in 2016 by former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair, places its own advisers inside presidents' and prime ministers' offices, where they help set policy while being paid by the institute and its donors. It absorbed Blair's Africa Governance Initiative, and in 2026 reported work with governments in more than 45 countries and about 1,000 staff. Its largest donor is the foundation of US tech billionaire Larry Ellison, which means a private donor funds advisers sitting inside foreign governments.
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia summary of TBI's published work

orgs.d: Pentecostal, charismatic and evangelical Protestant churches get their members and pastors into legislatures and governments and organise them there as voting blocs; this generic key is used when no single named church is the vehicle. In Brazil they sit as the Evangelical Parliamentary Front, with 213 deputies and 26 senators in the current legislature; President Bolsonaro put a Presbyterian pastor on the Supreme Court, and pastors without official posts steered education funds in return for bribes. In Africa they supply heads of government and ministers, as with Pentecostal preacher Abiy Ahmed in Ethiopia and a cleric given a new religious-affairs ministry in Zambia. Each case record names the specific church.

orgs.n: Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (IURD)
orgs.d: The Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (IURD), a neo-Pentecostal church founded in Rio de Janeiro in 1977 by Edir Macedo and run from the top, built its own political party to get its clergy into office: its pastors founded the Republicanos party in 2005, whose president Marcos Pereira is a church bishop. Its bishops have held federal ministries and the mayoralty of Rio. Abroad it has faced bans or state takeovers: Zambia banned it in 1998 and 2005 (both lifted on appeal) and Angola removed its Brazilian leadership in 2020.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Universal Church of the Kingdom of God' and 'Republicanos'
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia article (bans, investigations and press reports by country; Crivella's mission in South Africa)

orgs.hq: Redemption City of God, Mowe, Ogun State
orgs.d: The Redeemed Christian Church of God, a Nigerian holiness Pentecostal church founded in 1952 by Josiah Akindayomi, had one of its senior pastors in Nigeria's second-highest office: Yemi Osinbajo, senior pastor of its Lagos Province 48, was Vice President of Nigeria from 2015 to 2023. The church reports a presence in 197 countries and territories and over 5 million members in Nigeria.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Redeemed Christian Church of God' and 'Yemi Osinbajo'

orgs.d: Family Watch International (FWI), an Arizona-based Christian lobbying group founded in 1999 by Sharon Slater, uses its UN consultative status and contacts with African lawmakers to push laws against abortion, sex education and homosexuality. A Ugandan activist named Slater as having lobbied for Uganda's 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act, which sets life imprisonment and, in some cases, death. FWI had earlier called its position on the 2009 version of the bill 'complicated'. The law took effect, and the World Bank halted new lending to Uganda in August 2023 over it.

The Mourides are a Sufi Muslim brotherhood founded in Senegal in 1883 by Amadou Bamba, and their caliph (spiritual leader) trades religious backing for state support and influence. Their holy city, Touba, has run with wide autonomy from the state since 1928. Abdou Diouf received a voting instruction (ndigal) from the caliph in 1988. Abdoulaye Wade, a Mouride, went to Touba the day after his 2000 election and put Mourides in his government. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye visited Caliph Serigne Mountakha Mbacké on 7 August 2025, a visit before the annual Grand Magal pilgrimage that has become customary for heads of state.

The Qadiriyya Boutchichiya is Morocco's largest Sufi order, with several hundred thousand followers, and one of its followers has run the state's religious ministry for over two decades. Ahmed Toufiq, a historian, has been the king's Minister of Islamic Affairs, which oversees Morocco's mosques, since November 2002, under five prime ministers. He has said a chance meeting with the order's sheikh set him on the Sufi path. The Moroccan state promotes Sufism as an alternative to Salafism. In August 2025 a leaked letter from Toufiq warned the order about 'abuses' and 'appetites' during a dispute over its leadership.

orgs.n: Hereditary Sufi shrine lineages (pirs / makhdooms) of Pakistan
orgs.d: Families that hold hereditary custody of Sufi shrines in Pakistan (pirs or makhdooms, religious lineages whose devotees follow their guidance) turn devotees' loyalty into votes and send family members into national cabinets. Shah Mahmood Qureshi, custodian of the Bahauddin Zakariya shrine in Multan, was foreign minister twice. The shrines also give these families income from offerings, which supports their political careers. This is a generic key for such lineages.

Nahdlatul Ulama (NU), Indonesia's largest Muslim organisation, has moved its own leaders into the top offices of the state. Abdurrahman Wahid, NU's chairman from 1984 to 1999, founded the National Awakening Party (PKB), dominated by NU members, in 1998 and was elected president by the People's Consultative Assembly in October 1999. Ma'ruf Amin, NU's supreme leader from 2015, became Vice President in 2019. Founded in 1926 by traditionalist scholars and merchants and organised around pesantren (Islamic boarding schools), NU had over 40 million members in 2023 and was itself a political party from the 1950s to the 1970s.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Nahdlatul Ulama' and 'Ma'ruf Amin'; Wikipedia 'Abdurrahman Wahid'

orgs.d: The Knights of Columbus, a Catholic men's fraternal order (a membership society with lodges, here called councils) and insurance provider founded in New Haven in 1882, counts holders of high office among its members, including President John F. Kennedy and Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito. Its policy positions became an issue in the 2018–19 Senate confirmation of judge Brian Buescher, when senators asked whether membership would shape his rulings. It has councils in the United States, the Philippines and other countries.

orgs.hq: Network without headquarters (founder C. Peter Wagner)
orgs.d: The New Apostolic Reformation, a loose network of charismatic Christian 'apostles' and 'prophets' shaped by C. Peter Wagner, teaches that Christians should take control of government as one of seven spheres of society (the 'Seven Mountains' teaching); Wagner's 2008 book 'Dominion!' urged gaining political influence. Scholars say its standing grew after Trump's 2016 election. Wikipedia's account lists House Speaker Mike Johnson, Pennsylvania state senator Doug Mastriano and White House Faith Office head Paula White among associated figures.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'New Apostolic Reformation', citing André Gagné (2024) and others

orgs.d: Jesus Is Lord Church Worldwide, a Philippine Pentecostal church begun in 1978 by Eddie Villanueva with a Bible-study group at the Polytechnic University of the Philippines, has put its founding family into Congress. Villanueva ran for president in 2004 and 2010 and was a Deputy Speaker of the House from 2019 to 2022, and his son Joel Villanueva is a senator. Villanueva also founded the Philippines for Jesus Movement, a group of more than forty bishops.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Eddie Villanueva' and 'Jesus Is Lord Church'

orgs.n: Operation Rubicon / Thesaurus (CIA–BND ownership of Crypto AG)
orgs.d: The US CIA and West Germany's BND intelligence services secretly owned the Swiss company Crypto AG, which sold encryption machines to governments, and used it to read the coded messages of its government customers in more than 120 countries. The BND was co-owner from 1970 until about 1993 and the CIA until about 2018; the operation was called Thesaurus, later Rubicon. The Washington Post, ZDF and SRF revealed it on 11 February 2020, and the Swiss parliament held an inquiry the same year.
orgs.cite: Washington Post/ZDF/SRF, 11 Feb 2020; Swiss parliamentary inquiry 2020

orgs.d: Saudi Arabia's government recruited a Twitter employee, Ahmad Abouammo, and paid him to look up private data about critics of the kingdom who used the platform and pass it on. Officials around Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman thus had an insider at a foreign company who could reveal who was behind anonymous accounts. The FBI investigated, and a US jury convicted Abouammo in 2022.
orgs.cite: US v. Abouammo (N.D. Cal. 2022); Saudi anti-corruption committee statement 2019

orgs.d: North Korea places programmers inside foreign companies by having them take remote jobs under stolen or fake identities, mostly working from China and Russia, and their wages fund the state's weapons programmes. Paid facilitators run 'laptop farms', houses full of company laptops that make the workers appear to be in the employer's country. US prosecutors have found workers at hundreds of US firms in cases from 2024 to 2026, and Google reported a move into Europe in 2025.
orgs.cite: US Department of Justice cases 2024–26; Google Threat Intelligence Group, Apr 2025

orgs.d: China's Ministry of State Security, its civilian intelligence ministry, runs officers who recruit employees of foreign companies to hand over company secrets. One officer, Xu Yanjun, was convicted in the US in 2021 of trying to obtain aviation technology from GE Aviation through an employee. The ministry is also widely credited with the Salt Typhoon intrusions into telecom companies in some 80 countries, described in a 13-country joint advisory in August 2025.
orgs.cite: US v. Xu Yanjun (S.D. Ohio 2021); 13-country joint advisory Aug 2025

orgs.d: The US National Security Agency (NSA), the country's signals-intelligence agency, paid the security company RSA $10 million to make Dual_EC, a random-number generator the NSA had designed with a weakness, the default in RSA's software, Reuters reported in December 2013. Random numbers are used to create encryption keys, so a predictable generator can let someone read encrypted traffic, and RSA's customers used the weak default without knowing. The same weakness was used in the backdoor found in Juniper's ScreenOS network software in 2015.
orgs.cite: Juniper advisory Dec 2015; Checkoway et al.; Reuters, 20 December 2013, as reported by The Register, 21 December 2013

orgs.n: Russian intelligence services (FSB, GRU) acting through companies and insiders
orgs.d: Russia's security service (FSB) and military intelligence (GRU) reach into companies by recruiting employees, as courts found at SoftBank in Japan in 2020 and at chip firms ASML and NXP in the Netherlands in 2025. The US Commerce Department acted in 2024 over suspected access through the software maker Kaspersky, and the services have also used pressure in corporate disputes, as against the investment firm Baring Vostok in 2019.
orgs.cite: Court records in Japan and the Netherlands; US Commerce Department 2024

orgs.d: Jan Marsalek, chief operating officer of the German payments company Wirecard until June 2020, is described by German investigators and the UK Crown Prosecution Service as working for Russian intelligence while he held that post. After fleeing to Russia he directed a Bulgarian spy cell in Britain, convicted in 2025, and received material from Austrian intelligence officer Egisto Ott, convicted in 2026, so the network reached both a large company and a national intelligence service.

orgs.n: Chinese state talent-recruitment plans (Thousand Talents and local equivalents)
orgs.d: China's state talent-recruitment plans, such as Thousand Talents and local equivalents, recruit scientists and engineers working in foreign companies, and US prosecutors have tied members to theft of their employers' secrets. GE engineer Xiaoqing Zheng, a Thousand Talents member, was convicted in 2022, and Google engineer Linwei Ding, who had applied to a Shanghai plan, was tried in 2026.
orgs.cite: US v. Zheng (N.D.N.Y. 2022); US v. Ding (N.D. Cal. 2026)

orgs.d: Rostec, Russia's state corporation for defence and industrial technology, worked through the former management of Ukrainian engine maker Motor Sich, Ukrainian prosecutors charge: the executives colluded with Rostec to supply engines for Russian military helicopters. The SBU (Ukraine's security service) and the Prosecutor General brought the charges in 2022–23, alleging that managers inside a Ukrainian company had kept supplying Russia's military.

orgs.n: Chinese Communist Party organisations inside companies
orgs.d: The Chinese Communist Party places its own organisations inside companies: under China's Company Law, any firm with three or more party members must set one up. 73.1% of private firms had one in 2018, all top state firms wrote the party's role into their charters (founding rules) in 2017, and some foreign joint ventures were asked to do the same, giving the party a voice in decisions at companies with foreign owners.
orgs.cite: PRC Company Law; CCP Organization Department; CSIS

orgs.n: IRGC business empire (Khatam al-Anbiya and IRGC foundations)
orgs.d: Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), the military force that guards the Islamic Republic, took control of the Telecommunication Company of Iran in 2009 when IRGC-linked foundations bought it, and its construction arm Khatam al-Anbiya controls more than 812 companies. The UN (2010), the US (2007) and the EU (2008) designated Khatam al-Anbiya, meaning they placed it on sanctions lists.

Chinese state-linked capital gained control of the Dutch chipmaker Nexperia through Wingtech Technology, a Shanghai-listed electronics company almost 30% of whose shares trace back to the Chinese state, which bought Nexperia in 2018 for US$3.6 billion. In October 2025 the Dutch economy ministry took over Nexperia's governance under the Goods Availability Act, reportedly to stop chip know-how and production moving to China. China responded by banning exports of Nexperia chips packaged there, causing shortages for European carmakers. The Netherlands suspended its order in November 2025, and in February 2026 a Dutch court ordered an investigation into mismanagement at Nexperia.
orgs.cite: Dutch Goods Availability Act order Oct 2025

orgs.d: Sinochem Holdings is a Chinese state-owned chemicals group that, through ChemChina (later merged into it), took control of the Italian tyre maker Pirelli in 2015, putting a foreign state company in charge of a major Italian firm. It still held about 37% of Pirelli in 2025. In 2023 the Italian government used its 'golden power' national-security powers, which let it block or limit foreign control of strategic companies, to limit Sinochem's say over Pirelli by a decree of 4 August 2023. In April 2025 Pirelli's board ruled, citing that decree, that Sinochem's control had ended.

Sinovel Wind Group, a Chinese wind-turbine maker, recruited an insider at the Austrian unit of its US supplier AMSC and used him to steal AMSC's turbine control software. AMSC, a US maker of wind-turbine electronics, was Sinovel's main supplier at the time. A federal jury in Wisconsin convicted Sinovel of the theft on 24 January 2018.
orgs.cite: US District Court W.D. Wisconsin, 24 Jan 2018

orgs.d: Chen Li-ming, a former TSMC engineer who joined the Taiwan unit of Japanese chip-equipment maker Tokyo Electron, repeatedly asked engineers still working at TSMC to give him secrets on the etching equipment used in its 2-nanometer chip process, so Tokyo Electron could improve its machines and win orders. A Taiwan court ruled on 27 April 2026, sentencing Chen to 10 years and the TSMC engineers to shorter terms, and fined Tokyo Electron Taiwan NT$150 million.
orgs.cite: Taiwan court judgment, 27 Apr 2026; Taipei Times, 28 April 2026

orgs.n: CHJS (Chengdu chip venture of Choi Jin-seok)
orgs.d: Choi Jin-seok, a former Samsung executive, set up the chip venture CHJS in Chengdu, China, with about US$340 million from the Chengdu city government, and recruited a large number of Korean chip experts from Samsung and others. Korean prosecutors say CHJS was built on Samsung plant plans and process data taken by those recruits, including its chief plant designer, a former Samsung senior researcher. Police valued the leaked technology at 4.3 trillion won (about $3.2 billion).
orgs.cite: Seoul prosecutors 2023–24; The Korea Times, 10 September 2024

orgs.d: The Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC), Brazil's largest criminal organisation, which began in São Paulo's prisons and now trades cocaine internationally, gets its money and control inside legitimate companies, including fuel, fintech and transport firms. In Operação Fim da Linha on 9 April 2024, São Paulo prosecutors accused directors of the city bus operators Transwolff and UpBus, which held public transport contracts, of laundering money for the PCC. The city placed both companies under its own management the same day and later moved to cancel their contracts.
orgs.cite: São Paulo Public Ministry, Operação Fim da Linha 2024; Diário do Transporte, 9 April 2024

orgs.d: Cosa Nostra, the Sicilian Mafia, made up of family clans, placed its firms inside the supply contracts of Lidl Italia, the Italian arm of the German supermarket chain: a Milan court found in 2017 that the Laudani clan of Catania had done so in Lombardy. Prosecutors said clan-linked cooperative consortia, which handled logistics, security and store fit-outs, won orders by paying bribes to former Lidl officials and branch managers. Four Lidl regional directorates were placed under court administration for six months in May 2017; Lidl itself was not under investigation.

The 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, took over and steered construction and haulage firms in Emilia-Romagna in northern Italy through the Grande Aracri clan from Cutro, which had settled in the region by 2004 at the latest. Prosecutors said local businessmen turned to the clan to evade taxes, raise cash and win contracts, including for rebuilding after the 2012 earthquake, and alleged efforts to sway local elections. Bologna's anti-mafia prosecutors made 160 arrests on the night of 28–29 January 2015, leading to the Aemilia trial, the largest mafia trial in northern Italy. The Court of Cassation upheld the findings in rulings in 2018 and 2022.
orgs.cite: Court of Cassation, Aemilia rulings 2018 and 2022; Il Post, 'Il processo Aemilia', 21 October 2018

orgs.d: The yakuza are Japan's organised-crime groups, such as the Yamaguchi-gumi and Sumiyoshi-kai, and they placed workers inside the subcontracting chains of Japan's taxpayer-funded radiation clean-up after the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster, taking part of the workers' pay. The clean-up, worth about $35 billion, runs through layers of subcontractors. Police arrested yakuza members at least three times in 2012 for illegally placing workers under the construction company Obayashi; in 2013 a Sumiyoshi-kai member was arrested for taking about a third of the pay of men he sent. Reuters found gang-linked recruiters supplying homeless men from Sendai station.

South Africa's 'construction mafia' are extortion groups calling themselves 'business forums' that demand a cut, often 30%, of public building projects and try to capture ward councillors, the local elected officials, by bribery, threats or joining local party branches, the Institute for Security Studies (ISS) reported in October 2021. Forums shut down sites that refuse to pay; the contractors' body SAFCEC estimated at least R25.5 billion of projects had been disrupted or halted by March 2019. The ISS said three Tshwane councillors had been killed in under four years in killings linked to such groups. Prosecutors agreed to charge violent extortion under organised-crime law.

orgs.n: Ransomware and data-extortion groups that recruit insiders
orgs.d: Ransomware and data-extortion groups, criminal gangs often based in Russia, bribe or recruit company employees and contractors to plant malicious software or copy customer data, then demand ransom. In 2020 a Russian, Egor Kriuchkov, offered a Tesla employee money to install malware and was convicted in the US in 2021; in 2025 Coinbase disclosed that criminals had paid support contractors to copy customer data.
orgs.cite: US v. Kriuchkov (D. Nev. 2021); Coinbase disclosure 2025

orgs.d: Boeing, the US maker of airliners and military aircraft, has its own employees do much of the safety certification of its planes on behalf of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the US air-safety regulator, under a scheme called Organization Designation Authorization. That puts company staff in the regulator's seat when its own aircraft are checked. Congressional and Inspector General inquiries after the 737 MAX crashes of 2018–2019 found Boeing withheld information from the FAA, which therefore approved the plane without knowing what Boeing knew.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Purdue Pharma, the Sackler-owned maker of the opioid painkiller OxyContin, paid Practice Fusion, a company whose electronic health-record software doctors use during consultations, from about April to December 2016, in exchange for Practice Fusion steering prescriptions of Purdue's long-acting opioids. Practice Fusion built on-screen alerts nudging doctors to prescribe them, without saying a drug maker had paid for them. Purdue pleaded guilty in 2020 to federal charges including two counts of conspiracy to break the anti-kickback law, after an earlier 2007 plea for misbranding OxyContin. It went through bankruptcy and is being restructured.
orgs.cite: US DOJ press release on Purdue global resolution, 21 October 2020; CNBC, 28 January 2020; Reuters via Insurance Journal, 29 January 2020
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.n: US drug distribution industry (McKesson, Cardinal Health, AmerisourceBergen/Cencora)
orgs.d: The three largest US wholesale drug distributors (McKesson, Cardinal Health and AmerisourceBergen/Cencora) and their trade association hired former staff of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the agency that polices opioid supply, and one of them helped write the law that curbed it. Reporting in 2017 by the Washington Post and CBS 60 Minutes found that former DEA lawyer Linden Barber, who later joined Cardinal Health, 'wrote the Marino bill', which became a 2016 law making it harder for the DEA to freeze suspicious drug shipments. The industry spent over $102 million lobbying Congress on it and related bills in 2014–16.
orgs.cite: Washington Post, 'The drug industry's triumph over the DEA', 15 October 2017
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Monsanto, maker of the herbicide Roundup (glyphosate) and genetically modified (GM) seeds, paid a senior Indonesian environment ministry official $50,000 in 2002, through a consulting firm it had hired, to drop the requirement for an environmental impact study before GM cotton could be grown. Monsanto admitted it in a 2005 US settlement and paid $1 million to the Justice Department and $500,000 to the SEC. US court documents also show its contacts with an EPA manager, and Germany's glyphosate review reproduced industry text. Bayer bought Monsanto in 2018.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Consultants working for Florida Power & Light (FPL), Florida's largest electric utility, are tied to a scheme to change who won state Senate seats. Nonprofits partly overseen by the head of FPL's consulting firm Matrix LLC supplied about $630,000 of the roughly $730,000 in dark money (political spending whose donors are hidden) behind 'ghost' candidates in the 2020 Florida Senate races. The little-known candidates were recruited to split the vote; in District 37 the incumbent lost by under 40 votes. Reporting by Floodlight and Mother Jones in 2024 traced the money. Several people were convicted or pleaded no contest. FPL was not charged, denies wrongdoing and says two law firms cleared it.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.n: Elon Musk's companies (Tesla, SpaceX, Neuralink, xAI)
orgs.d: Elon Musk, who controls Tesla, SpaceX, Neuralink and xAI, led the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), a White House operation to cut federal spending and staff, in 2025, while federal agencies were pursuing enforcement actions against those companies. This put the owner of regulated companies inside the government that regulates and buys from them. A US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations minority staff memo (from the opposition party's staff) estimated $2.37 billion in potential liabilities for his companies at stake in those actions.
orgs.cite: US Senate PSI minority staff memorandum, 27 April 2025
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: The Coca-Cola Company, the world's largest soft-drink maker, built channels into public-health agencies. Its executive Alex Malaspina founded the International Life Sciences Institute (ILSI), an industry-funded science body, in 1978. Emails released under the Freedom of Information Act show that in 2015 Malaspina asked Barbara Bowman, then head of heart disease and stroke prevention at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), how to approach the World Health Organization about its push to curb sugary drinks, and she suggested contacts. Bowman left the CDC in 2016.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: The International Life Sciences Institute (ILSI), a nutrition and food-safety science body funded by food, drink and chemical companies and founded by a Coca-Cola executive, had its China branch operate from inside China's Center for Disease Control and Prevention, the government agency that advises on diet and obesity policy. Academic research by Susan Greenhalgh, published in the BMJ in 2019, found this gave member companies a voice in Chinese nutrition policy. Mars left ILSI in 2018 and Coca-Cola in 2021.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Randox Laboratories, a Northern Ireland diagnostics company, paid Owen Paterson, a sitting Conservative MP and former cabinet minister, as a consultant, and he then lobbied government regulators and ministers on its behalf. The Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards, who polices MPs' conduct, found in 2021 that this was paid advocacy, which is banned for MPs. After the government first tried to overturn the finding, Paterson resigned as an MP in November 2021.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: PPE Medpro, a company set up in May 2020 and linked to Conservative peer (House of Lords member) Michelle Mone and her husband Doug Barrowman, won £200 million of Covid protective-equipment contracts after Mone referred it to the government's 'VIP lane', a fast track for suppliers recommended by ministers, MPs and peers. Mone denied any link for years, then admitted in December 2023 that she stood to benefit. The High Court ordered PPE Medpro in 2025 to repay about £122 million for supplying gowns that did not meet the contract.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.n: Association for Financial Markets in Europe (AFME)
orgs.d: The Association for Financial Markets in Europe (AFME), the lobby group for large banks in European capital markets, hired Adam Farkas, executive director of the European Banking Authority (EBA), the EU body that writes banking rules, as its chief executive in 2020, while he still had access to the regulator's confidential information. The European Ombudsman, who investigates EU bodies, ruled on 11 May 2020 that the EBA's failure to forbid the move was maladministration (improper administration).
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Servier, the French drug company that sold Mediator (benfluorex), hired former officials of the drug regulator as paid advisers. A Paris court in 2021 convicted Jean-Michel Alexandre, former director of drug evaluation at the national medicines agency, of an illegal conflict of interest for advising Servier, and gave him an 18-month suspended sentence and a €30,000 fine. The same trial convicted Servier of deception and manslaughter over Mediator, which damaged heart valves, and fined the agency itself €303,000 for withdrawing the drug only in 2009.
orgs.cite: Prescrire International, June 2021; Que Choisir, 29 March 2021
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Novartis, the Swiss drug company, paid employees of Greek state-owned or state-controlled hospitals and clinics to prescribe its drugs, through paid trips to overseas medical congresses in 2012–2015 and a sham study in 2009–2010. In June 2020 Novartis paid about $347 million in the US to settle bribery charges under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, which covers this Greek conduct and other cases. Separate Greek claims that Novartis bribed politicians were dropped.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Shell, the Anglo-Dutch oil and gas company, had its own people working inside the Nigerian government. A 2009 US diplomatic cable records a Shell executive saying the company had seconded (loaned) staff to all the relevant Nigerian ministries, giving it knowledge of officials' moves. In the Netherlands, government memos released in 2018 show Shell lobbied in 2017 for abolishing the dividend tax. In the OPL 245 case over a Nigerian oil block, a Milan court acquitted Shell and Eni of bribery in 2021.
orgs.cite: WikiLeaks cable 2009; Dutch government memos 2018; Milan Tribunal 2021
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Agrofert, a Czech agriculture, food and chemicals group founded by Andrej Babiš, stayed under his control while he was Czech prime minister, the office that oversees how EU farm and development subsidies are paid out, including to Agrofert. A 2021 European Commission audit found he still controlled the group through trust funds despite claiming to have given it up, a conflict of interest under EU rules. He placed Agrofert in a new trust in February 2026.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: A group around Timur Mindich, a businessman and co-owner of the Kvartal 95 studio, is accused by Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) of running 'shadow managers' inside Energoatom, Ukraine's state nuclear power company. NABU says they made contractors pay kickbacks of 10–15% of contract values to avoid blocked payments, and laundered about $100 million. NABU announced the case, called Operation Midas, in November 2025; former energy minister Herman Halushchenko was named a suspect and suspended as justice minister.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Electrogas, the consortium that built and runs Malta's Delimara gas power station under a government contract, had as a director Yorgen Fenech, who owned a secret Dubai company, 17 Black. Leaked emails listed 17 Black as an expected source of income for secret Panama companies set up by energy minister Konrad Mizzi and the prime minister's chief of staff, Keith Schembri. Fenech faces corruption charges with a former minister and chief of staff in the Maltese courts in 2025–2026.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Shaul Elovitch, who formerly controlled Bezeq, Israel's largest telecoms company, and owned the Walla! news site, is accused of having Walla! give Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu favourable coverage in exchange for regulatory decisions worth hundreds of millions of shekels. Netanyahu was also communications minister, the post that regulates Bezeq. The indictment says he removed a ministry director-general who opposed Elovitch's requests. Elovitch is co-defendant with Netanyahu in this bribery case, Case 4000, under a 2020 indictment; both deny wrongdoing.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Telia Company, the Swedish-Finnish telecoms group (TeliaSonera until 2016), paid bribes to companies belonging to the daughter of Uzbekistan's president, who had influence over the government body that issued telecoms licences, to enter and stay in the Uzbek mobile market. In 2017 Telia paid about $965 million to settle US Justice Department and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) bribery cases.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Airbus, the European maker of airliners and military aircraft, paid bribes through outside agents and consultants to officials and executives of its customers, including state airlines, to win aircraft orders. The UK case covered Sri Lanka, Malaysia, Indonesia, Taiwan and Ghana in 2011–2015. In 2020 Airbus paid about €3.6 billion under deferred prosecution agreements (deals in which charges are suspended if the company pays and reforms) in France, the UK and the US.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: BAE Systems, Britain's largest arms maker and prime contractor on the Al-Yamamah arms sales to Saudi Arabia, admitted giving 'substantial benefits' to a Saudi public official who could influence its fighter-jet sales. It also admitted making more than $150 million in payments through an offshore British Virgin Islands company that were likely used to sway foreign governments' decisions. BAE pleaded guilty in the US in 2010 to conspiracy and paid $400 million.
orgs.cite: SEC Actions, 'BAE Systems pleads guilty to FCPA violations', March 2010
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Rolls-Royce Holdings, the British aero-engine maker, paid bribes to win orders in several countries, which it admitted in 2017 settlements with UK, US and Brazilian prosecutors. In Indonesia its money reached the chief executive of Garuda Indonesia, the state-owned airline, which bought its engines. The Jakarta Corruption Court jailed the Garuda chief in 2020.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Samsung Group, South Korea's largest business group, reached the presidency through money paid by its head, Lee Jae-yong, to Choi Soon-sil, the close friend and unofficial adviser of President Park Geun-hye, in return for government backing for his takeover of the group from his father. Seoul courts convicted Lee of bribery between 2017 and 2021; the scandal also led to Park's impeachment. Lee was pardoned in 2022.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO), operator of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant, used its close ties with its regulators to weaken safety rules before the 2011 tsunami and meltdowns. The Japanese parliament's (Diet's) independent commission found in July 2012 that the regulator had been captured: it described collusion between TEPCO, regulators and the government, said TEPCO 'manipulated its cozy relationship with regulators to take the teeth out of regulations', and called the disaster man-made. It recommended a new, independent regulator.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia, 'National Diet of Japan Fukushima Nuclear Accident Independent Investigation Commission'
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Leonardo, the Italian defence group (formerly Finmeccanica), is accused through its helicopter maker AgustaWestland of paying bribes, through middlemen, to Indian officials to win a contract for VVIP helicopters (aircraft for India's top leaders). In 2017 India's Central Bureau of Investigation charged former air force chief S.P. Tyagi in the case, which is still pending, and middleman Christian Michel has also been charged. In Italy, Leonardo's former chief Giuseppe Orsi was acquitted in 2019.
orgs.cite: Hindustan Times, 2 September 2017; The Quint, September 2020
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), the UAE's state oil company, had its chief executive, Sultan Al Jaber, preside over COP28, the UN's annual climate conference, in 2023. That put an oil company head in charge of the talks meant to cut fossil-fuel use. Leaked briefing papers reported by the BBC and the Centre for Climate Reporting in 2023 showed his COP28 team planned to raise oil and gas deals in meetings with foreign governments; Al Jaber denied it.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.n: State Oil Company of Azerbaijan Republic (SOCAR)
orgs.d: People from Azerbaijan's state oil and gas company, SOCAR, led COP29, the 2024 UN climate conference in Baku where countries negotiate cutting fossil-fuel use. Its president, ecology minister Mukhtar Babayev, was a former SOCAR vice-president who had worked there for more than 24 years, to 2018; Global Witness called his January 2024 appointment 'a bad case of déjà vu'. The summit's chief executive, deputy energy minister Elnur Soltanov, sat on SOCAR's board, and Global Witness secretly filmed him discussing investment in SOCAR gas fields with a man posing as an investor; the BBC reported the recording on 8 November 2024. This put the host's oil industry at the head of talks meant to reduce its product.
orgs.cite: Global Witness, 2024; CNBC, 8 January 2024; BBC / Global Witness, 8 November 2024 (via MyJoyOnline)
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.n: Fossil fuel industry delegations at UN climate talks
orgs.d: Lobbyists for oil, gas and coal companies and their trade associations are accredited to UN climate summits, some as members of government delegations, which gives them access to the negotiations. The Kick Big Polluters Out coalition counts them each year from UN participant lists and found at least 2,456 at COP28 in 2023. At COP28, France's delegation included TotalEnergies and EDF, Italy's included Eni, and the European Union's included staff of BP, Eni and ExxonMobil.
orgs.cite: Corporate Europe Observatory / Kick Big Polluters Out, 5 December 2023
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Philip Morris International, the world's largest listed tobacco company outside China, tried to shape the WHO tobacco treaty (Framework Convention on Tobacco Control) by getting finance, trade and agriculture officials, rather than health officials, onto national delegations. Leaked documents reported by Reuters on 13 July 2017 show this goal. Reuters found the ratio of health to finance delegates fell from over six in 2006 to just over three in 2016. The treaty's secretariat asked Vietnam in 2015 to exclude tobacco industry employees from its delegation. Philip Morris also lost treaty claims against Uruguay (ICSID 2016) and Australia (PCA 2015).
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: British American Tobacco (BAT), the second-largest listed tobacco company, is shown by leaked records to have paid government officials in East and Central Africa, with the aim of weakening tobacco-control laws and gaining advantage over rivals. The records were reported by BBC Panorama in 2015 and researchers at the University of Bath in 2021. The UK Serious Fraud Office closed its investigation in 2021 without charges.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.n: International Chamber of Shipping (with BIMCO and World Shipping Council)
orgs.d: The International Chamber of Shipping, the main global shipowners' association, working with BIMCO and the World Shipping Council, has members inside the national delegations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), the UN body that sets shipping rules. InfluenceMap found in 2017 that the Chamber led industry efforts to delay climate rules, that 31 of 100 member states at one environment committee meeting brought business representatives in their delegations, and that five delegations were led by commercial ship registries.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: ABB, the Swiss-Swedish engineering group, paid over $37 million in bribes to an official at Eskom, South Africa's state electricity company, to win contracts at the Kusile coal power station, a large coal-fired plant Eskom was building. The payments bought the official's help from inside the state company. ABB admitted it in December 2022 settlements with the US Justice Department and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: SAP SE, the German business-software maker, paid bribes to government officials in South Africa and Indonesia to win public contracts. In January 2024 it agreed a deferred prosecution agreement with the US Justice Department, a deal in which charges are suspended if the company pays and reforms, and paid over $220 million in total.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Bosasa (later African Global Operations), a South African facilities and services firm run by Gavin Watson, won prison contracts after paying officials and politicians. The Zondo commission, the state inquiry into corruption and 'state capture', found in 2022 that Bosasa had influenced officials to get its contracts. The company went into liquidation in 2019.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Thales Group (formerly Thomson-CSF), the French defence and electronics group, paid Jacob Zuma, then South Africa's deputy president, an annual R500,000 through his financial adviser Schabir Shaik, starting in 2000, to protect it from investigation into the 1999 arms deal and help it win future tenders. Shaik was convicted of corruption and fraud in 2005 and sentenced to 15 years. Thales is co-accused with Zuma before the Pietermaritzburg High Court; the trial began in 2020 and is unresolved.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Process & Industrial Developments Ltd (P&ID) paid Grace Taiga, legal director of Nigeria's Ministry of Petroleum Resources, while it negotiated a 2010 gas-processing contract with the ministry; one payment came 11 days before signing. When the deal collapsed, P&ID won an $11 billion arbitration award against Nigeria. The High Court of England and Wales set the award aside in October 2023, finding it had been obtained by fraud and bribery.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Italian prosecutors charged that Eni, Italy's state-controlled oil company, and Shell used the price of a Nigerian oil block to pay bribes to Nigerian officials. In 2011 Eni and Shell paid $1.1 billion through a Nigerian government account for the offshore block OPL 245, and the money went on to Malabu Oil and Gas, a company controlled by former oil minister Dan Etete. Prosecutors charged both companies and executives, including Eni chief executive Claudio Descalzi, with international corruption. On 17 March 2021 a Milan court acquitted all defendants, and in 2022 prosecutors dropped their appeal, so the bribery claim is unproven.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: BSG Resources, the mining arm of Beny Steinmetz's group, won rights to the Simandou iron-ore deposit in Guinea by bribing a wife of President Lansana Conté, who used her position to influence the decision. Simandou is one of the world's largest untapped iron-ore deposits. A Geneva Criminal Court found in 2021 that the rights were won through these bribes and convicted Steinmetz of corruption.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Companies of Israeli investor Dan Gertler, including Fleurette and Ventora, held Congolese mining and oil assets. The US Treasury said in December 2017 that Gertler used his close friendship with DR Congo's President Joseph Kabila to act as middleman for state mining asset sales, which went cheaply to offshore companies tied to him. Congo reportedly lost over $1.36 billion in revenue in 2010–2012. The Treasury sanctioned him and his companies.
orgs.cite: US Treasury press release sm0417, 21 December 2017
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Sakunda Holdings, the Zimbabwean fuel, mining and agriculture group founded by Kudakwashe Tagwirei, grew through his relationship with President Emmerson Mnangagwa and other officials. The US Treasury said in 2020 that Tagwirei used these ties to win government deals and preferential access to foreign currency, and gave luxury vehicles to senior officials. The US (2020, 2024) and UK (2021) sanctioned him. Tagwirei became a cabinet minister in October 2026.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms equipment maker, paid bribes to government officials and others to win contracts in Djibouti, China, Vietnam, Indonesia and Kuwait, often through middlemen and sham consultancy contracts. It admitted this in a 2019 settlement with the US Justice Department and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) worth over $1 billion.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Sociedad Química y Minera (SQM), the Chilean lithium and fertiliser miner, paid Chilean politicians and their campaigns for years, disguised as payments for services recorded on fake invoices. The payments came to light in Chilean investigations from 2015. In 2017 SQM settled US charges under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, which bans paying foreign officials, through a deferred prosecution agreement.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: JBS, the world's largest meat company, and its parent J&F Investimentos, controlled by brothers Joesley and Wesley Batista, paid politicians for favours. In 2017 the Batistas gave plea testimony and secret recordings to prosecutors, including a recording of President Michel Temer, which led the Prosecutor-General to charge Temer with corruption that year.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Construction, energy and transport companies in Argentina paid cash to officials of the Kirchner governments in return for public-works contracts, according to the Notebooks case (Cuadernos), named after a government driver's notebooks recording cash deliveries. Their executives are on trial with former president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner at the Federal Oral Court since 2025; several testified as 'repentants', meaning cooperating defendants.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Vitol, the largest independent oil trader, paid bribes to officials of state oil companies in Brazil (Petrobras), Ecuador (Petroecuador) and Mexico (Pemex) to win contracts to buy and sell their oil and fuel. The payments bought insiders who steered state business to Vitol. Vitol paid $135 million to US authorities in 2020, and a former Vitol trader was convicted in 2024.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Instituto Pensar Agro (IPA), a think tank funded by 48 agribusiness associations, drafts the legislative agenda of Brazil's Agricultural Parliamentary Front, the cross-party farm caucus in Congress. Member firms include Bayer, BASF, Syngenta, Cargill and JBS. This lets companies write the bills that sitting legislators then put forward. The arrangement was documented by De Olho nos Ruralistas in July 2022.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Glenn Defense Marine Asia, the Singapore ship-husbanding contractor (a company that supplies fuel, food and port services to visiting ships) run by Leonard Francis, bribed US Navy officers with cash, gifts and prostitutes for years. In return officers passed it classified ship schedules and steered ships to ports where it overcharged. 22 people pleaded guilty and Francis was sentenced to 15 years in 2024 in the US District Court for southern California.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.n: Italian mafia groups (Cosa Nostra, 'Ndrangheta, Camorra, Puglia clans)
orgs.d: Italian mafia-type groups, as defined by article 416-bis of the criminal code (Cosa Nostra, the 'Ndrangheta, the Camorra and Puglia clans), get their people and influence into local councils, steering contracts and permits. Italy's Law 164/1991 lets the government dissolve a council found to be conditioned by such a group and send in commissioners. Il Sole 24 Ore counted 402 dissolution decrees from 1991 to September 2025.
orgs.cite: Il Sole 24 Ore count of dissolution decrees, December 2025

orgs.d: The Camorra, the network of clans in Naples and Campania, reached into national government. The Casalesi clan of Caserta controlled construction and waste businesses, and former economy undersecretary Nicola Cosentino was finally convicted by the Court of Cassation on 27 April 2023 of external complicity with it, meaning he helped the clan without formally belonging. Campania has many councils dissolved for mafia infiltration.

orgs.n: Bari and Puglia clans (Parisi, Strisciuglio, Montani)
orgs.d: Clans of Bari and wider Puglia (Parisi, Strisciuglio, Montani), sometimes grouped with the Sacra Corona Unita, have members inside public bodies. In 2024 Parisi clan members working at AMTAB, Bari's city transport company, were charged with extortion, and a councillor's husband is on trial for buying clan votes. Puglia accounts for 26 council dissolutions for mafia infiltration since 1991.

Mafia Capitale ('Mondo di mezzo'), a network led by Massimo Carminati and Salvatore Buzzi, bribed Rome city officials and politicians to win city contracts, including for services to migrants, from about 1999 to 2014. Rome prosecutors brought the case in 2014. The Court of Cassation ruled it was not a mafia-type association, but corruption convictions stand.

orgs.n: Hong Kong and Macau triads (14K, Sun Yee On, Wo Shing Wo)
orgs.d: Wan Kuok-koi ('Broken Tooth'), former leader of the 14K triad in Macau (triads are Chinese secret-society crime groups), got a seat on the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, the Communist Party's political advisory body. The US Treasury revealed this when it sanctioned him in December 2020, together with his World Hongmen History and Culture Association, which it called a front for crime, and his Dongmei Group. A crime boss thus sat inside a state advisory body while building projects in Myanmar's scam zones and in Palau. Other Hong Kong and Macau triads include Sun Yee On and Wo Shing Wo.
orgs.reach_src: cases in this file and Wan Kuok-koi's Wikipedia entry

orgs.n: Kokang crime families (Bai, Ming, Wei, Liu)
orgs.d: Crime families (Bai, Ming, Wei, Liu) ran the government of Myanmar's Kokang Self-Administered Zone and its scam and gambling centres in Laukkai. Bai Suocheng was the zone's first head from 2011 to 2016 and a Shan State MP. After the 2023 rebel offensive, leaders were handed to China; Chinese courts sentenced Bai and Ming family members to death and executed 11 Ming members and four Bai group members in early 2026.

orgs.n: Karen Border Guard Force / Karen National Army (Saw Chit Thu)
orgs.d: The Karen Border Guard Force, renamed the Karen National Army in 2024, is a Karen militia placed under the Myanmar army in 2010, and Chinese-run crime groups partnered with its leader, Colonel Saw Chit Thu, to build scam centres. In 2017 he partnered with She Zhijiang's Yatai group to build Shwe Kokko and dealt with Wan Kuok-koi's Dongmei Group over Saixigang; Wan, a former 14K triad leader, was sanctioned by the US in 2020. The junta gave Saw Chit Thu its Thiri Pyanchi honour in November 2022. The UK and then the US sanctioned him for links to forced labour in scam centres.

orgs.n: Chinese Unification Promotion Party and Bamboo Union
orgs.d: The Chinese Unification Promotion Party (CUPP), founded in 2005 by former Bamboo Union triad leader Chang An-lo, has members who recruited Taiwanese military officers for Chinese intelligence. In 2025 Taiwan's Kaohsiung High Court sentenced CUPP deputy secretary-general Wen Lung and two retired officers for trying to recruit serving personnel. Taiwan's Interior Ministry says the party works with China on espionage and election interference and links 98 organised-crime cases to its members since 2010. It said in July 2026 it would ask the Constitutional Court to dissolve the party.

Pemuda Pancasila (Pancasila Youth), an Indonesian paramilitary organisation founded in 1959, puts its members into Indonesia's parliament and party leadership. It took part in the 1965–66 killings, supported Suharto and was part of the Golkar party from 1982 to 2001. In 2024, 48 of its cadres were elected to the House of Representatives and 14 to the Regional Representative Council; its deputy chairman Bambang Soesatyo was speaker of the People's Consultative Assembly. Members are known for extortion and protection work. It was shown in the 2012 film The Act of Killing.

In India, local strongmen and gang leaders get themselves elected to state and national legislatures, which gives them influence over police and local government. This is not one organisation; an example is Mukhtar Ansari in Uttar Pradesh. The Association for Democratic Reforms, an election watchdog, found 46% of MPs elected in 2024 declared pending criminal cases.
orgs.cite: Association for Democratic Reforms; Indian courts

orgs.d: The Peoples' Aman Committee, a gang from Lyari in Karachi led by Rehman Dakait and then Uzair Baloch, worked inside the ruling Pakistan Peoples Party's (PPP) local machinery. A Sindh government joint investigation team (JIT) report released in 2020 records Uzair Baloch saying that, with the then provincial home minister's help, he got his chosen police chiefs posted in Lyari and party tickets for his nominees in the 2013 election. The PPP denies this. The group was banned; a military court sentenced Uzair Baloch in 2020.

The brothers of Afghanistan's two top leaders were among the insiders who drained Kabul Bank, the country's largest private bank, which paid soldiers, police and civil servants. Its shareholders included Mahmood Karzai, brother of President Hamid Karzai, and Abdul Haseen Fahim, brother of First Vice-President Mohammad Qasim Fahim, and the bank gave millions to a presidential campaign against central bank advice. A 2012 anti-corruption committee report found close to $900 million taken, with most loans going to 19 people and companies. The founder and chief executive were jailed for five years; the two brothers were not charged. The state relaunched the bank as New Kabul Bank in 2011.
orgs.cite: Afghan special tribunal; anti-corruption monitoring committee
orgs.reach_src: cases in this file and Wikipedia

orgs.d: The Nour Zuhair network took about $2.5 billion from Iraq's General Commission for Taxes in 2021–22 through 247 cheques paid to front companies, which needed officials inside the commission and the government to approve them. A Baghdad court convicted 10 people in late 2024, including aides of former Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi, whose office was supposed to oversee such payments.

Haiti's armed gangs, which joined in the Viv Ansanm alliance in 2023, have people inside the state, according to the UN Security Council's panel of experts in a report released in October 2026. The panel says at least one member of a new Cité Soleil municipal commission is an active gang member and that some police officers supply gangs with weapons and information. It accuses former legislator Alfredo Junior Antoine of arming groups and sponsoring a 2025 attack that killed more than 100 people, and former senator Nenel Cassy of controlling a criminal group in Miragoâne; both deny it.
orgs.cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti; Global Affairs Canada

orgs.d: Rio de Janeiro's militias (milícias), armed groups made up largely of current and former police officers, control territory in west and north Rio, selling 'protection', gas, transport and land, and their members and allies have held elected office. Brazil's Supreme Federal Court convicted two politicians in 2026 of ordering the 2018 murder of city councillor Marielle Franco, who had investigated militias.

Los Dinámicos del Centro is a network that prosecutors say sold driving licences from inside the transport office of Peru's Junín regional government from 2012, and passed the money to the Perú Libre party. Selling licences this way meant regional officials issued them for payment rather than on test results. The Junín Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office has investigated the network since 2021.

The Rizzuto family, Montreal's Mafia, took a share of the city's public construction contracts through firms that also paid political parties, witnesses told a Quebec public inquiry. The Charbonneau Commission (2011–2015) investigated collusion and corruption in public construction contracts and organised-crime infiltration of the industry. During the inquiry Montreal mayor Gérald Tremblay resigned, and interim mayor Michael Applebaum and Laval mayor Gilles Vaillancourt were later convicted or pleaded guilty in related corruption cases. The commission reported on 24 November 2015.

Italian-American crime families, including New York's Five Families, took control of waterfront hiring, union locals and construction rackets (organised extortion schemes), deciding who worked on the docks and taking a cut. The bi-state Waterfront Commission was created in 1953 to license dock workers and curb their hold on the port of New York and New Jersey; it was dissolved in 2023. Federal prosecutions have repeatedly charged families over this control.
orgs.cite: Waterfront Commission Compact; US federal prosecutions

orgs.d: Australian outlaw motorcycle ('bikie') gangs such as the Hells Angels, Comancheros, Mongols and Rebels, active in drugs, firearms and extortion, had members holding roles in the construction division of the CFMEU, a union that bargains with building companies. Reports in 2024, including the Watson report, found this, and the federal government put the division into administration (control by an appointed administrator).
orgs.cite: Federal administration of the CFMEU (2024); Watson report

orgs.n: Swedish criminal networks (Foxtrot, Rumba and others)
orgs.d: Sweden's criminal networks, such as Foxtrot and Rumba, which drive a high rate of shootings and bombings, get people and influence inside public bodies. Research for the think tank SNS in 2023 ('The Vulnerable State') found them infiltrating government agencies, welfare-sector companies and the social insurance system, through employees and bribes, with municipalities especially exposed.

A group of businessmen, police officers and officials is accused of colluding with South Africa's Police Minister to protect its interests. KwaZulu-Natal police commissioner Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi alleged in July 2025 that Minister Senzo Mchunu had disbanded a task team investigating political killings to shield the syndicate; Mchunu denies it. The Madlanga Commission, a judicial inquiry, is examining the claims, and 13 officers had been charged by mid-2026.
orgs.cite: Daily Maverick, 6 July 2025; Mail & Guardian, 6 July 2025

orgs.n: Black Axe and the Neo Black Movement of Africa
orgs.d: Black Axe is a Nigerian confraternity, a secretive brotherhood founded at the University of Benin in 1977, that police in several countries treat as an organised-crime group, and the BBC linked it to a group given government jobs after election work. Leaked documents in a December 2021 BBC Africa Eye investigation suggested the Neo Black Movement of Africa (NBM) was paid 35 million naira to 'protect votes' in the 2012 Edo State governorship election and then given 80 government roles. Former members told the BBC that members hold posts in state assemblies and are hired by politicians for election violence. The NBM denies any link to Black Axe.

Jos Leijdekkers ('Bolle Jos'), a Dutch fugitive sentenced in absentia in Rotterdam in 2024 to 24 years for smuggling over 7 tonnes of cocaine, has protection inside Sierra Leone's ruling circle, Reuters reported on 25 January 2025, citing three sources and video. Two sources said he is married to President Julius Maada Bio's daughter Agnes, and footage shows him two rows behind the president at a New Year's Day mass. Sierra Leone said it was investigating and dismissed its head of immigration; the government denies knowing where he is.

Westwood Company Ltd, a Gambian firm that held the exclusive rosewood export licence, was co-founded by the country's own president, Yahya Jammeh, with Swiss national Nicolae Bogdan Buzaianu, according to TRIAL International. The president's office therefore awarded the licence to a company he part-owned. Gambia exported about $163 million of rosewood, mostly from Senegal's Casamance, to China in 2014–17.

Samherji, an Icelandic fishing company, paid people close to Namibia's government, including two ministers, to obtain fishing quotas, the state-issued rights to catch set amounts of fish, which those ministers' offices controlled. The payments were exposed in the 2019 Fishrot Files, leaked company documents. Namibia charged the two ministers under organised-crime law, and Iceland opened an investigation.

A cigarette and narcotics smuggling network led by Miloš Medenica was protected from inside Montenegro's judiciary by his mother, Vesna Medenica, former president of the Supreme Court, who used her position to shield it from investigation and prosecution. A Supreme Court president heads the country's highest court and has influence over the wider judiciary. The High Court in Podgorica sentenced both in January 2026.

Albanian crime groups, active in drug trafficking in Albania, Italy, the UK and the Netherlands, have links to people elected to office. Albania's 2015 decriminalisation law, which bars people with criminal records from public office, removed seven MPs, three mayors and about 600 officials who had hidden their records, showing how far people with criminal pasts had reached into elected office.
orgs.cite: Albanian Central Election Commission; Exit News

orgs.d: The 'Drenica Group' is the name a 2010 Council of Europe report gave to a criminal group of former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) commanders that it said was led by Kosovo's own Prime Minister, Hashim Thaçi. Swiss senator Dick Marty told the Council's Parliamentary Assembly in December 2010 that the group controlled criminal trades including heroin, and found 'credible, convergent indications' of organ trafficking after the 1999 war. The Assembly endorsed the report in January 2011; Thaçi denied it. An EU task force later led to the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, where Thaçi has been on trial for war crimes since 2023. The organised-crime claims have not been tested in court.

A network around Martin Bozhanov, known as 'the Notary', is alleged to have gathered compromising material on Bulgarian judges and prosecutors, which could be used to pressure them over cases. This would give the network leverage inside Bulgaria's courts and prosecution service. The allegations are under investigation; Bulgarian National Radio and the state news agency BTA have reported them.

Vlad Plahotniuc, a businessman and leader of the Democratic Party of Moldova, built a business and political network that was described as controlling Moldova's government and parliamentary majority until 2019, which put a party leader's business interests in charge of the state. The bank theft he was tried for drained money that the state later had to cover. A Chișinău court convicted him in April 2026 over the 2014 theft of about $1 billion from Moldovan banks.

The Global (Russian) Laundromat moved $20–80 billion out of Russia in 2010–14 by using Moldovan judges inside the court system: they enforced fake debts, giving the transfers legal cover. The money then went through Moldindconbank and Latvian banks to companies worldwide. OCCRP, the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta exposed the scheme.

The gang led by Sergei Tsapok in Kushchyovskaya, Krasnodar Krai, operated for years under the protection of local authorities, and Tsapok himself sat as a deputy on the district council. In November 2010 it murdered 12 people. The case showed how a gang could run a district while its leader held elected office there. Tsapok was convicted and died in prison in 2014.

Gangs in Chongqing, a large city in south-west China, were protected by senior police officers, who used their posts to shield the gangs from investigation. The city's 2009–11 crackdown arrested 4,781 suspects, including six district police chiefs, and the former deputy police head Wen Qiang was executed in 2010 for protecting gangs.

orgs.n: Rothschild family banks (N M Rothschild & Sons; Rothschild & Co)
orgs.hq: New Court, St Swithin's Lane, London; Paris
orgs.d: The Rothschild banks are the family banking houses founded by Mayer Amschel Rothschild's sons, and several French bankers have moved from them into the top of the French state. Georges Pompidou was general manager of Banque Rothschild from 1956 to 1962, then Prime Minister and, from 1969, President. Emmanuel Macron was a Rothschild partner before becoming Economy Minister in 2014 and President in 2017. François Pérol advised Banque Populaire at Rothschild, followed its merger from the Élysée, then headed the merged bank, BPCE; he was acquitted of illegal taking of interest. No court has found the bank directed their policies.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Rothschild family', 'Rothschild & Co'; N. Ferguson, The House of Rothschild (1998)

orgs.hq: 23 Wall Street (historic); 270 Park Avenue, New York
orgs.d: J.P. Morgan & Co., the New York private bank, placed its partners in public office and its men on company boards. Partners Thomas Lamont, Dwight Morrow, Russell Leffingwell and S. Parker Gilbert held top public posts; Lamont sat on the US reparations team at Versailles. In 1913 the Pujo Committee, a congressional inquiry into banking power, found Morgan-linked men held 341 directorships in 112 corporations. The bank was also Britain's and France's agent in the US in 1914–17. Its successor JPMorgan Chase paid $264 million in 2016 for hiring relatives of Chinese officials to win business, and former JPMorgan bankers now run Argentina's economy ministry and central bank.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'J. P. Morgan', 'JPMorgan Chase', 'Pujo Committee'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope pp. 52–53

orgs.d: Paul Warburg, a partner of the New York investment bank Kuhn, Loeb & Co., secretly helped write the plan for the US central bank and then sat on its first board. In 1910 Warburg joined Senator Nelson Aldrich and other bankers at the Jekyll Island Club in Georgia, where they drafted the Aldrich Plan; it was published without naming its authors and laid the ground for the Federal Reserve. In 1914 Warburg was appointed to the first Federal Reserve Board, the body that oversees the banks. The secret drafting became public when fellow participant Frank Vanderlip described the meeting in the Saturday Evening Post in February 1935. Antisemitic writers later falsely claimed the firm financed the Bolsheviks. It merged with Lehman Brothers in 1977.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Jacob Schiff', 'Paul Warburg'; P. Roberts, American Jewish Archives Journal 49 (1997); Saturday Evening Post, 'Jekyll Island and the Secret Behind the Fed' (Vanderlip, 9 Feb 1935)

orgs.d: M. M. Warburg & Co. is a Hamburg private bank founded in 1798, and its head Max Warburg, who ran it from 1910 to 1938, moved between the bank and German state posts. He served as an expert at the 1919 Versailles peace talks, where his partner Carl Melchior became principal delegate for economic questions on his recommendation, and sat on the general council of the Reichsbank, Germany's central bank, from 1924. The Nazis forced him off the council because he was Jewish and 'Aryanised' the bank in 1938. In 2016 a €47 million cum-ex tax claim against the bank was dropped after its co-owner met Hamburg mayor Olaf Scholz.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'M. M. Warburg & Co.'; German Wikipedia 'Max Warburg'

orgs.d: Historian Carroll Quigley describes the London partners of Lazard, an investment bank with houses in New York, Paris and London, as part of the Milner/Round Table group, a private British policy network that placed its people in state posts. Quigley writes that Lazard Brothers' Robert Kindersley sat on the 1924 Dawes committee on German reparations, and that Robert Brand moved Lazard men Adam Marris and Thomas Brand into Britain's wartime Washington embassy and supply boards; that account is Quigley's. Later, Lazard partner Felix Rohatyn ran New York City's 1975 financial rescue, and the firm advised the UK on the 2013 Royal Mail sale, in which its fund arm also took shares.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Lazard'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment; NAO (2014)

orgs.d: A member of the Barings banking family ran the finances of a country the bank lent to. Barings, a London merchant bank founded in 1762, held a significant stake in Egyptian debt when Evelyn Baring (later Lord Cromer) became Britain's financial controller of Egypt after the Khedive's 1876 bankruptcy, the post that oversaw repayment to European creditors; no conflict of interest was raised at the time. From 1883 to 1907 he was Britain's agent and consul-general, the real ruler of Egypt. Barings also financed the Louisiana Purchase (1803) with Hope & Co., was rescued in 1890 after Argentine losses, and collapsed in 1995 after Nick Leeson's £827 million trading losses; ING bought it for £1.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Barings Bank', 'Evelyn Baring, 1st Earl of Cromer'

orgs.n: Wallenberg family sphere (Stockholms Enskilda Bank, SEB, Investor AB)
orgs.d: The Wallenbergs are a Swedish banking and industrial family whose Stockholms Enskilda Bank held German-owned companies on paper during the Second World War so that the German firm Bosch kept control of them. In 1939–41 the bank bought Bosch subsidiaries, including the American Bosch Corporation, on condition that Bosch could buy them back after the war. The US treated this as 'cloaking', hiding the real owner behind a front, seized American Bosch in 1943 and blacklisted the bank from 1945 to 1947. At the same time the bank's heads led Sweden's trade talks: Jacob Wallenberg with Germany, Marcus Wallenberg Jr. with Britain.

Credit Suisse, a Swiss bank taken over by UBS in 2023, arranged secret state-guaranteed loans to Mozambique in 2013–14 in a scheme in which bribes reached Mozambican officials and the bank's own staff. Three state companies borrowed $622 million from Credit Suisse and $535 million from Russia's VTB, backed by state guarantees never shown to parliament or the IMF, for projects with the shipbuilder Privinvest. The US Justice Department said at least $200 million went in bribes and kickbacks to bankers and officials. Credit Suisse pleaded guilty to wire fraud in the US in 2021, was fined almost $500 million and forgave $200 million of Mozambique's debt.

BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, was hired to run US public rescue programmes while its own executives moved into top government posts. The US Treasury retained it in 2009, and in March 2020 the Federal Reserve chose it to manage its $500 billion and other corporate bond-buying programmes. In 2021 Brian Deese, BlackRock's former global head of sustainable investing, became director of President Biden's National Economic Council, which coordinates economic policy. In Germany, Friedrich Merz chaired BlackRock's German arm from 2016 to 2020, returned to parliament in 2021 and was elected Chancellor in May 2025.

Citigroup, the US bank formed in 1998, had an executive draw up a new president's cabinet before the election. On 6 October 2008 Michael Froman, who had followed Robert Rubin from the Treasury to Citigroup, emailed John Podesta of Barack Obama's transition team from his Citigroup address with candidate lists for 31 cabinet-level posts; the email came out only when WikiLeaks published Podesta's emails in 2016. The New Republic found the list largely matched the appointments. Rubin had joined Citigroup in 1999, the year the Glass–Steagall separation of commercial and investment banking was repealed, which made the merger legal. Froman joined the White House in 2009, and Citigroup received a federal rescue in 2008.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Robert Rubin', 'Michael Froman'; The New Republic, 14 Oct 2016

orgs.d: Banco Rural, a Brazilian bank owned by the Rabello family, supplied the cash used to pay members of Congress for their votes in the 'mensalão' (big monthly payment) scheme of 2005. Large withdrawals from its branches in Brasília and Belo Horizonte, made through firms of publicist Marcos Valério, went to deputies, their relatives or advisers so that they would back the Workers' Party government. In 2012 Brazil's Supreme Federal Court convicted the bank's president, Kátia Rabello, of money laundering and other crimes. The Central Bank of Brazil put the bank into liquidation in 2013.
orgs.cite: Supreme Federal Court AP 470; Portuguese Wikipedia 'Kátia Rabello'

orgs.n: Banco Espírito Santo / Grupo Espírito Santo
orgs.d: Banco Espírito Santo (BES) was the Portuguese bank of the Espírito Santo family, led by Ricardo Salgado, nicknamed 'Dono Disto Tudo' ('owner of all this'). In the Operation Marquês case, prosecutors link Espírito Santo group payments to former Prime Minister José Sócrates, saying the head of government received undue money, and charge Salgado with corruption. A judge threw out most charges in 2021, an appeal court reinstated them in 2024 and the trial began in July 2025; the defendants are presumed innocent. The bank collapsed in August 2014 and its good assets became Novo Banco.

In Lebanon, politicians and their families own most of the large commercial banks, which in turn lent heavily to the state those politicians ran. A 2016 study by economist Jad Chaaban found that 18 of the 20 largest banks had major shareholders linked to political elites, holding about 43% of the sector's assets, and that this affected the banks' lending and their exposure to public debt. The banks financed the state and the central bank, the Banque du Liban, under governor Riad Salameh, until the system collapsed in 2019 and froze depositors' savings.

The CIA, the US foreign intelligence agency, and West Germany's BND intelligence service secretly owned the Swiss company Crypto AG, whose cipher machines more than 120 governments used to protect their messages. The two services bought it in 1970; the BND left around 1993 and the CIA remained owner until 2018. The machines were rigged so the services could read customers' communications, while those governments believed they were buying from a neutral Swiss firm. A Swiss parliamentary inquiry confirmed the arrangement in 2020.
orgs.cite: Swiss parliamentary inquiry 2020; Trump statement Oct 2025

orgs.d: Crypto AG was a Swiss maker of cipher machines (devices that encrypt messages) that was secretly owned by the CIA and West Germany's BND intelligence service, so that the two agencies could read the messages of the governments that bought them. More than 120 governments were customers. The BND co-owned it from 1970 until about 1993 and the CIA until 2018, when the firm was liquidated. The machines were deliberately weakened. A Swiss parliamentary inquiry confirmed the secret ownership in 2020.
reach_est: more than 120 customer states, not all named

orgs.d: India's foreign intelligence agency, the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), cultivated Australian politicians and a state police service and recruited an Australian with a security clearance, according to Australia's security service ASIO. In a 2021 speech ASIO chief Mike Burgess described a foreign 'nest of spies' that did this and also monitored a diaspora community. In April 2024 Australian media and the Washington Post reported that the country was India and that two RAW officers were expelled in 2020. A RAW officer was also charged in the US over a plot to murder Sikh activist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun.
orgs.reach_src: cases in this file and existing records

orgs.d: Pakistan's main military intelligence agency, the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), secretly funded lobbying of the US Congress and, the US says, used a militant group as its own arm inside Afghanistan's Taliban. US prosecutors said the ISI paid at least $3.5 million to Ghulam Nabi Fai's Kashmiri American Council in Washington to lobby officials and make political donations; Fai pleaded guilty in 2011. That year the top US military officer, Admiral Mike Mullen, called the Haqqani network the ISI's 'veritable arm'; after 2021 its leader Sirajuddin Haqqani became the Taliban government's interior minister. Pakistan denies the ties.
