Egypt's main intelligence service, the General Intelligence Service (GIS), had an agent working inside the German government's press office, which handles the chancellor's communications. German federal prosecutors charged the employee in November 2020 with working for the GIS since 2010, reporting on German media coverage and helping an attempt to recruit a further source, in return for favours for his family.

Cuba's foreign intelligence service, the Intelligence Directorate (DI, formerly DGI), recruited people who rose inside the US government and helped run Venezuela's military counterintelligence. It recruited Ana Montes, who became the Defense Intelligence Agency's senior Cuba analyst and spied for Havana until her 2001 arrest; she was convicted in 2002. Former US ambassador Víctor Manuel Rocha also served Cuban intelligence. Under 2008 agreements seen by Reuters, Cuba's defence ministry oversaw the restructuring of Venezuela's military counterintelligence, which turned to watching Venezuela's own officers.
orgs.reach_src: cases in this file and existing records

orgs.d: North Korea's main foreign intelligence and cyber body, the Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB), places North Korean IT workers under false identities in jobs inside foreign companies to earn money for the state, according to US agencies. One US 'laptop farm' let such workers appear to be working from the US for more than 300 American companies, earning over $17 million; its American operator was jailed for eight years in 2025. US agencies also tie the RGB to the 2016 theft of $81 million from Bangladesh's central bank through fraudulent SWIFT payment orders sent from inside the bank's network.

Russia's domestic security service, the FSB, got inside the anti-doping testing at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics to hide Russian athletes' drug use. The McLaren reports, commissioned by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) in 2016, found a 'state-directed' system in which FSB-linked staff, working with Russia's sports ministry and the WADA-accredited Moscow laboratory, opened supposedly tamper-proof sample bottles and swapped athletes' urine. The findings led to sanctions on Russian sport.

The National Intelligence Service (NIS), formerly the KCIA, is South Korea's intelligence agency, and US prosecutors charged that it recruited a Washington foreign-policy expert to work for it. Sue Mi Terry, a former CIA analyst and fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, a leading US think tank, was indicted in July 2024 as an unregistered foreign agent acting for the NIS since 2013. Prosecutors said she passed notes from a 2022 private meeting with Secretary of State Antony Blinken and wrote op-eds at NIS request, in return for designer goods and over $37,000 for her programmes. In October 2026 the charges were deferred; she acknowledged contacts but no wrongdoing.

A network linked to the Srivastava Group, an Indian company group, used UN-accredited NGOs to get speakers into the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, where they promoted Indian interests and criticised Pakistan, according to EU DisinfoLab, a Brussels research group. NGOs with UN accreditation may speak at Council sessions. EU DisinfoLab exposed the network in 2019 and in December 2020 as 'Indian Chronicles': it revived dead NGOs, impersonated dead rights activists, ran hundreds of fake local news sites and also worked on the European Parliament. EU DisinfoLab did not show that the Indian government directed it.

The Iran Experts Initiative was a project of Iran's Foreign Ministry, begun in 2014, to cultivate Iranian-heritage academics at Western think tanks, research groups that advise governments, so that they would promote Tehran's positions. Leaked ministry emails reported by Semafor and Iran International in September 2023 revealed it and said it was proposed by diplomat Saeed Khatibzadeh. Pentagon official Ariane Tabatabai was linked to it, and House Armed Services chairman Mike Rogers objected. In October 2023 the Pentagon said she had been properly vetted and kept her security clearance.

The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) is the foundation, run jointly by the Olympic movement and governments, that sets drug-testing rules for world sport, and Russia's FSB security service and Ministry of Sport worked through a WADA-accredited laboratory to hide doped athletes. Richard McLaren's reports for WADA in 2016 found a 'state-directed failsafe system' involving the ministry, the FSB and the Moscow laboratory. FSB-linked staff opened supposedly tamper-proof sample bottles at the 2014 Sochi Olympics to swap urine. More than 1,000 Russian competitors benefited between 2011 and 2015, and at least 643 positive samples were hidden. Russian military intelligence hackers later attacked WADA.

World Athletics (formerly the IAAF), the governing body of track and field based in Monaco, had its president paid by Russian interests to hide Russian athletes' doping. Lamine Diack led it from 1999 to 2015. In September 2020 a Paris court convicted him of corruption for helping cover up Russian doping in return for money; about €3.2 million was extorted from suspected dopers so they could compete at London 2012.

The UN Secretariat in New York and UN offices such as the human rights office (OHCHR) in Geneva have been pressed or reached by member states. In 2016 Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon removed the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen from his list of parties that kill and maim children, citing 'undue pressure' from supporters who threatened to stop funding UN programmes; Saudi Arabia denied making threats. An OHCHR staff member, Emma Reilly, alleged the office confirmed to China the names of Chinese activists attending UN meetings; OHCHR rejected her claims. Snowden documents also showed the NSA got into the UN's internal video system in 2012.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, the permanent court that tries individuals for genocide and war crimes, was spied on and its prosecutors privately pressured by Israeli intelligence for nearly a decade, according to a May 2024 investigation by the Guardian, +972 Magazine and Local Call. It reported that Mossad director Yossi Cohen pressed prosecutor Fatou Bensouda before she opened a Palestine investigation, and that the communications of Bensouda and her successor Karim Khan were intercepted. Israel denied the claims.

Countries that sell citizenship or passports have let buyers pay their way into political circles and diplomatic posts. Al Jazeera reported in 2019 that an Iranian donor to Dominica's prime minister was given an ambassadorship and diplomatic passport, and that in Grenada businessmen were offered diplomatic posts; both governments deny wrongdoing. In the 2020 'Cyprus Papers', the Speaker of the House was filmed offering to help a convicted money launderer get a passport. In Comoros, ex-president Sambi was convicted in 2022 over the sale of passports to stateless Gulf residents (bidoon), and FinCEN warned in 2014 that sanctioned Iranians had bought St Kitts passports.
orgs.cite: FinCEN FIN-2014-A004; Al Jazeera Investigative Unit; OCCRP

orgs.d: Companies linked to UK businessman Zuneth Sattar won Malawi police and army contracts by paying officials, according to Malawi's Anti-Corruption Bureau. Its June 2022 report said five companies linked to him won 16 contracts worth over 150 million dollars from the police and the Malawi Defence Force in 2017–2021. The Bureau later arrested Vice President Saulos Chilima, accusing him of receiving about $280,000 and other items from Sattar in 2021 in return for helping two Sattar companies get government contracts. President Chakwera withdrew Chilima's delegated powers; Chilima denied wrongdoing and died in a plane crash in June 2024.
orgs.cite: Malawi ACB report, June 2022; TheCable / AFP, 'Malawi vice-president arrested over $280,000 bribery allegation', Nov 2022; VOA, 25 Nov 2022

orgs.d: Groups moving South American cocaine to Europe and the US, including Colombia's FARC rebels, have bought or recruited military and security chiefs in transit countries. In Guinea-Bissau, former navy chief José Américo Bubo Na Tchuto was arrested in a US sting in 2013 and pleaded guilty, and army chief Antonio Indjai was indicted for offering to store FARC cocaine. In Suriname, Dino Bouterse, head of the counter-terrorism unit and son of the president, was convicted in New York and sentenced in 2015 to about 16 years.

orgs.n: Benjamin Bol Mel and his companies
orgs.d: Benjamin Bol Mel, a South Sudanese businessman, moved from winning government contracts to holding the state's top offices. His company, ABMC Thai-South Sudan Construction, received government road contracts worth tens of millions of dollars without competitive bidding while he was President Salva Kiir's principal financial adviser and private secretary. The US sanctioned him for corruption on 21 December 2017. He was named one of South Sudan's vice presidents and deputy secretary general of the ruling SPLM on 10 February 2025, and was removed from both posts by decree on 12 November 2025.

Burmeister & Wain Scandinavian Contractor, a Danish power-plant builder, paid officials of the Mauritian administration through intermediaries during tenders for the Saint-Louis power station of the state Central Electricity Board, the African Development Bank found. In June 2020 the bank, which lends for such projects, debarred the company from its contracts for 21 months.

Al-Qaeda, the jihadist network founded by Osama bin Laden, has members inside Afghanistan's Taliban government, according to UN monitors. The UN Security Council's sanctions Monitoring Team assessed in 2023 that at least three key leaders in the Taliban government are affiliated with al-Qaeda, and its reports through 2025 say the group keeps close ties with the Taliban and a presence in several provinces.

orgs.n: Zhao Wei Transnational Criminal Organization (Kings Romans)
orgs.d: The Zhao Wei Transnational Criminal Organization, a Chinese-led casino group (Kings Romans), runs a Lao government economic zone. Under a 99-year lease from Laos from 2007, Zhao Wei's group set up and administers the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Bokeo province. In 2018 the US Treasury designated the group for drug trafficking and money laundering through the zone, meaning US persons may not deal with it; the UN drugs office has linked the zone to cyber-fraud compounds.

orgs.n: VimpelCom, Telia and MTS (Uzbek telecom bribery)
orgs.d: Three telecom groups, VimpelCom, Telia and MTS, paid companies controlled by Gulnara Karimova, the Uzbek president's daughter, to get into Uzbekistan's mobile market. In US foreign-bribery settlements in 2016, 2017 and 2019 the firms admitted the payments, agreeing to pay 795, 965 and 850 million dollars respectively. Uzbek prosecutors put her kickbacks at 869.3 million dollars; she was convicted in Uzbekistan in 2017 and 2020.

orgs.n: Cary Yan and Gina Zhou (Rongelap SAR scheme)
orgs.d: Cary Yan and Gina Zhou, China-born businesspeople, paid Marshall Islands legislators and other officials from 2016 to 2020 to pass a law creating a semi-autonomous 'Rongelap Atoll Special Administrative Region' that they would shape. Both pleaded guilty to bribery in New York and were sentenced in 2023, Yan to 42 months.

Getax Australia, a Gold Coast phosphate trader, is charged by Australian federal prosecutors with conspiring to bribe Nauruan politicians between 2007 and 2012 to win phosphate deals; the case has been repeatedly delayed and the charges are unproven. In a related case, Sydney businessman Mozammil Bhojani pleaded guilty to paying over 120,000 dollars to a Nauruan MP and a minister and was jailed in 2018.

Firms paid by Australia's Home Affairs department to run asylum centres on Nauru and Manus Island passed money to Nauruan and Papua New Guinea political figures, a 2023 Sydney Morning Herald and Age investigation reported. It found millions in subcontracts going to firms tied to Nauru's leaders, including over 120,000 dollars in suspect payments to justice minister David Adeang, who denies wrongdoing; the reporters said they were not claiming the payments were bribes. A former Paladin director said a 1.5 million dollar invoice marked 'Visas' on the Manus contract was a bribe, which Paladin's former chief executive denies.

The Habilaj family ran an Albanian-Italian cannabis-trafficking group, and its link reached Albania's interior minister, Saimir Tahiri, who was in charge of the police and is a cousin of the family. Italian police arrested Moisi Habilaj in October 2017 in a probe into the group, which moved over 3.5 tonnes of cannabis, and wiretaps mentioned Tahiri. On 19 September 2019 Albania's Serious Crime Court convicted Tahiri of abuse of office and sentenced him to 3 years and 4 months, but dropped the drug-trafficking and organised-crime charges.

MOL, Hungary's state-influenced oil company, paid Croatia's prime minister to give it management control of Croatia's national oil company INA, according to Croatian courts. They found that Prime Minister Ivo Sanader took a 10 million euro bribe from MOL chief executive Zsolt Hernádi; the Supreme Court confirmed the conviction in 2021. Hungary has not handed Hernádi to Croatia, and MOL denies the bribe.

Yuri Borisov, a Russian businessman who ran the Lithuanian helicopter firm Avia Baltika, bought access to Lithuania's president with campaign money. He reportedly gave about 400,000 dollars to Rolandas Paksas's 2002 campaign and then received Lithuanian citizenship by Paksas's decree. In 2004 the Constitutional Court found Paksas had broken the constitution and his oath, and parliament removed him from office, the first European head of state impeached.

17 Black, a Dubai company owned by Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech, was named in leaked papers as a planned source of payments to secret Panama companies of the Maltese prime minister's chief of staff Keith Schembri and energy minister Konrad Mizzi. Journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia exposed the companies and was murdered in 2017; Fenech is charged with commissioning the killing. Schembri and Mizzi resigned, and a 2021 public inquiry found the state had created an 'atmosphere of impunity'.

Dmitry Rybolovlev, a Russian billionaire who owns AS Monaco football club, was suspected of courting Monaco officials, including the principality's former public prosecutor Jean-Pierre Dreno, to get favourable treatment in his legal disputes. The suspicion rested on messages found on the phone of his lawyer, Tetiana Bersheda. In November 2018 he was made a formal suspect in a corruption and influence-peddling probe, known as 'Monacogate'. The case was dismissed in 2023, and in February 2025 Monaco's courts closed it, ruling the phone data unlawfully obtained after a European Court of Human Rights finding.

In San Marino, business owners paid politicians for building permits and banking licences, with the bribes run through a bank account in the name of 'Giuseppe Mazzini', a 19th-century Italian patriot. Twenty-one former political figures, including former state secretaries, went on trial in 2015; several were convicted in 2017 and the convictions were upheld in 2022.

Patria, a Finnish state-owned defence company, was accused of paying bribes, partly aimed at Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša, to win a 2006 deal for armoured vehicles. A Ljubljana court convicted Janša in 2013, but the Constitutional Court annulled the verdict and the case lapsed. An Austrian court convicted a middleman, and two Patria executives were convicted in Finland over separate Croatian deals.

orgs.n: Stanford Financial Group / Stanford International Bank
orgs.d: Allen Stanford's offshore bank, Stanford International Bank in Antigua, bribed the island's chief financial regulator to look away from a 7 billion dollar fraud. A 2009 US indictment charges Leroy King, head of Antigua's Financial Services Regulatory Commission, with taking more than 100,000 dollars from Stanford to ignore the bank's real assets and obstruct a US investigation; Antigua extradited him in 2019. Stanford was convicted in the US.

MS-13 (Mara Salvatrucha), a transnational gang, made a secret deal with Salvadoran government and prison officials, according to a 2023 US indictment. It says officials gave the gang's jailed leaders benefits and released one wanted by the US, and in return the gang cut public killings and backed the governing Nuevas Ideas party in the 2021 election. The US sanctioned the prisons director in 2021 over the talks; President Bukele's government denies any pact.

Mohamed's Enterprise, a Guyanese gold trading firm of Nazar and Azruddin Mohamed, bribed customs and other officials, the US Treasury said when it sanctioned the family and firm in 2024. Treasury said they kept more than 10,000 kg of gold off customs declarations and evaded more than 50 million dollars in duty, paid officials for favourable treatment in court matters and bribed to win state contracts. It also sanctioned a home affairs ministry permanent secretary.

orgs.hq: London — first grand lodge, 1717; each country has its own grand lodges
orgs.d: Freemasonry, a fraternal order with private rituals organised in lodges, has had its members hold senior state and police posts, and in some countries the head of state also led the lodge. This dot gathers grand lodges not mapped separately. Presidents Omar Bongo of Gabon and Denis Sassou-Nguesso of Congo were reported grand masters, Iran's Grand Master Jafar Sharif-Emami twice served as prime minister, and in Liberia lodge membership was needed to lead the ruling party. Cuba's former grand master admitted he was a state-security officer. In the UK, judges and police were for a time required to declare membership, and in 2026 the High Court upheld the Metropolitan Police's rule that officers declare it.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Sovereign Order of the Initiatic Temple (OSTI)
orgs.d: The Sovereign Order of the Initiatic Temple (OSTI), an esoteric Templar order founded by Raymond Bernard, former head of the Rosicrucian order AMORC in France, received Cameroon state money through President Paul Biya. Le Monde reported in 1999 that Biya gave OSTI and its charity CIRCES tens of millions of francs in 1988–92, and that 11.2 million francs moved from the state oil company SNH to Bernard's own account. The presidency called Bernard an 'old friend' and did not comment on the payments.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: Shinto Seiji Renmei (Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership), the political arm of Japan's Association of Shinto Shrines, runs a league of Diet (parliament) members who back its aims, such as constitutional revision and official honours for Yasukuni Shrine; its members fill most cabinet seats. In 2014, 16 of the 19 members of Shinzo Abe's cabinet were listed supporters, and in 2025, 12 ministers of Sanae Takaichi's new cabinet belonged to its league. It works closely with Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: South Korea's intelligence agency, the KCIA, paid members of the US Congress in the 1970s through businessman Tongsun Park to keep US support for President Park Chung-hee's government. In 1978, under immunity, Park admitted giving money to 30 members. Former Representative Richard Hanna pleaded guilty and went to prison, and the House reprimanded three other members; former Representative Otto Passman was acquitted.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: PRC state proxies (United Front not named)
orgs.d: This dot gathers cases in which officials or intelligence officers of the People's Republic of China worked through local people inside other countries' institutions, where the record does not name the United Front Work Department (the Communist Party body for overseas influence). Cases include the mayor of Arcadia, California pleading guilty in 2026 as a PRC agent, a European Parliament member's aide jailed in Germany in 2025 for spying for China, a former New York police sergeant convicted in 2023 of helping China's 'Fox Hunt' campaign, and Chinese officers placed inside Pacific police forces.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: This dot gathers cases where foreign governments, rather than a single named organisation, paid, recruited or placed people inside another country's institutions. Cases include US Senator Bob Menendez, convicted in 2024 as an agent of Egypt; a Twitter manager convicted in 2022 of spying for Saudi Arabia; Hungary's EU mission running a spy ring against the European Commission; and Canada's parliamentary intelligence committee (NSICOP) finding some parliamentarians 'witting' in foreign interference.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: Organised white supremacist groups, such as the Klan and skinhead groups, have tried to get their members into police forces, the FBI warned. A 2006 FBI assessment described 'ghost skins' who hide their beliefs and said at least one group urged them to seek police jobs, which 'can lead to investigative breaches'. A 2015 FBI policy guide said investigations of such extremists had often found active links to law enforcement officers.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Order of the Star Spangled Banner (Know Nothings)
orgs.d: The Order of the Star Spangled Banner, a secret anti-immigrant fraternal order, built the Know Nothing movement and its American Party and took over a state government. In the 1854 Massachusetts election it won the governorship, all 40 state Senate seats and all but three House seats. The 1855 legislature passed laws to deport poor or mentally ill Irish residents, to 'inspect' Catholic schools and convents and to require Protestant Bible reading in public schools.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The Society of St. Tammany, a fraternal society with ritual offices called sachems, ran New York's Democratic Party machine and through it the city government. William M. 'Boss' Tweed became its Grand Sachem in 1863 and controlled the city while holding seats in Congress, the county board and the state Senate. A city committee in 1877 estimated he stole $25–45 million; he was convicted in 1873 on 204 of 220 counts.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The Loyal Orange Institution (Orange Order), a Protestant fraternal lodge, had its members fill Canadian city halls and federal office. Twenty of Toronto's 23 mayors in the 19th century and every mayor in the first half of the 20th century were Orangemen, and in 1942 16 of 23 city council members were. Four prime ministers, including Mackenzie Bowell, a past Grand Master, were Orangemen.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The Ordre de Jacques-Cartier, a secret French-Canadian Catholic society active from 1926 to 1965, worked by recruiting decision-makers and getting its members appointed to federal public-service jobs. Its members included Montreal mayor Jean Drapeau and politician Pierre Laporte, and it had about 11,300 members in 1955–56. It dissolved in 1965 after a former insider, Roger Cyr, exposed it in a 1964 book.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The Knights of Saint Columbanus, a Catholic fraternal order founded in Ireland in 1915 and long described as secretive, had members in Irish cabinets and the civil service. Taoiseach (prime minister) John A. Costello and other ministers in his 1948 government were Knights, and Justice Minister Seán MacEoin reportedly assured the order's Supreme Council that conflict between Church and State would be avoided. These accounts rest mainly on biographies by John Cooney (1999) and Anthony Jordan (2007).
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The Service d'Action Civique (SAC), a Gaullist security association created in 1960 and run in practice by Jacques Foccart, de Gaulle's adviser on Africa, was a parallel network that recruited police officers. Its Marseille leader was himself a police inspector, Jacques Massié, whom an SAC commando murdered with his family in 1981. A National Assembly inquiry followed and the government dissolved the SAC in 1982 under the law on private militias.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: Westland New Post, a Belgian far-right paramilitary group founded by Paul Latinus, had members inside the gendarmerie (national police) and a NATO site. A former gendarme said he was recruited into 'Group G', a neo-Nazi cell inside the gendarmerie linked to the group, and NATO documents passed on by a member from the Evere transmission centre were found at another member's home. Latinus had been an informant for Belgium's State Security service. A parliamentary inquiry found no proof of a conspiracy behind the Brabant killings.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The 'Patriotic Union' around Heinrich XIII Prinz Reuss, part of the Reichsbürger movement that rejects the modern German state, had a sitting judge, a former MP and special-forces soldiers among its members. Birgit Malsack-Winkemann, a Berlin judge and former AfD member of parliament, was to be its justice minister and led co-accused through the Reichstag twice in 2022. Federal prosecutors charged the group as a terrorist association planning to storm the parliament; trials began in 2024.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: Voice of Europe was a Prague-based pro-Russian news outlet that, Czech intelligence says, paid European politicians from Russian money supplied by Viktor Medvedchuk. The Czech government sanctioned it in March 2024. German prosecutors are investigating AfD politician Petr Bystroň over cash reportedly handed over in Prague, and both the Bundestag and, in May 2025, the European Parliament lifted his immunity; he denies the claims.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: Informationsbyrån (IB) was a secret Swedish military intelligence bureau with no official status that registered and infiltrated far-left groups, and it was reported to answer to leaders of the governing Social Democratic Party as well as to the military. Journalists Jan Guillou and Peter Bratt revealed it on 3 May 1973, including break-ins at the Communist Party's offices. Former security chief P. G. Vinge wrote that IB director Birger Elmér had regular contact with Prime Minister Olof Palme and reported to party secretary Sven Andersson; Palme denied any link. The journalists, not IB staff, were convicted of espionage in 1974. A 2002 public inquiry set out IB's operations.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The White Hand (Bela ruka), a secret Serbian officers' society founded in 1912 by Petar Živković, gained influence over the future King Alexander and put its leader in charge of government. Alexander suspended the constitution in 1929 with White Hand officers' support, and Živković was made prime minister, serving until 1932.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: P3 was a secret group, named by the press after the P2 lodge, that Italian prosecutors said sought undue influence on the state, including senior judges. In 2018 a Rome court convicted businessman Flavio Carboni and Arcangelo Martino under the 1982 Anselmi law, which bans secret associations, and gave a senior judge, Vincenzo Carbone, a suspended sentence for abuse of office.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: P4 is the press name for an information-trading network run by go-between Luigi Bisignani, which drew in officials who passed on confidential state information. In the 2011 inquiry, deputy and former prosecutor Alfonso Papa was accused of passing confidential information to Bisignani; he was convicted in 2016, but the charges lapsed on appeal. Bisignani took a plea of 1 year 7 months.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: In Italy, mafia groups such as the 'Ndrangheta have used 'covered' (secret) Masonic lodges to link up with officials, business and local government. A 2017 report by parliament's Anti-Mafia Commission found 193 lodge members recorded in organised-crime cases and that in Castelvetrano 4 of 5 town executives were Freemasons. In 2023 former senator Giancarlo Pittelli, described as a Freemason linking a clan to Masonic circles, was given 11 years for collusion.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: IDEA (Sacred Bond of Greek Officers), a secret society of army officers formed in 1945, placed its members at the head of the state through the 1967 coup. Several coup leaders, including Georgios Papadopoulos, were members, and IDEA members took key posts under the junta. In 1975 the junta leaders were convicted of high treason.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: Golden Dawn, a Greek neo-Nazi party that held up to 21 seats in parliament, had ties inside the police and was ruled a criminal organisation. In 2013 the Council of Europe's human rights commissioner said he had strong evidence of police links to the party, and after the 2012 election polling stations used by Attica police officers gave it just over 20% of the vote. In 2020 an Athens court convicted its leaders of running a criminal organisation, upheld on appeal in 2026.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

channels.n: Ambrosiano's offshore money: Milan → Nassau → Lima → Managua
channels.d: Roberto Calvi, chairman of Italy's Banco Ambrosiano, was a member of P2, a secret Masonic lodge run by Licio Gelli, and the Vatican Bank (IOR), the Holy See's own bank, was Ambrosiano's main shareholder. Calvi's bank ran its offshore business through Ambrosiano Overseas in Nassau and Banco Ambrosiano Andino in Lima, and money passed through them funded both the Somoza regime and the Sandinista opposition in Nicaragua. The IOR was tied to the offshore companies that held the money missing when the bank collapsed in 1982: $1.287 billion could not be accounted for. In April 1992 a Milan court convicted 33 people of fraud, and Gelli's 12-year sentence was confirmed in 1998.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Banco Ambrosiano'; Milan Tribunal verdict April 1992; Court of Cassation April 1998

channels.n: Vatican Bank's backing of Banco Ambrosiano: Vatican City → Milan
channels.d: The Vatican Bank (IOR), the Holy See's bank, was the main shareholder of Milan's Banco Ambrosiano, whose chairman Roberto Calvi belonged to the secret P2 Masonic lodge. Under its president, Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, the IOR allegedly issued letters of patronage, written assurances backing Ambrosiano's foreign units, and it was tied to the offshore companies that held the money missing when the bank collapsed in 1982. In February 1987 Milan magistrates sought the arrest of Marcinkus and two IOR officials, but Italy's top court ruled that the 1929 Lateran Treaty between Italy and the Holy See shielded them. The IOR denied legal liability, acknowledged 'moral involvement' and paid US$224 million to Ambrosiano's creditors.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Institute for the Works of Religion'; Italian Court of Cassation, Re Marcinkus, Mennini and De Strobel, 17 July 1987

channels.n: P2 lodge enrolled Argentina's rulers: Arezzo → Buenos Aires
channels.d: P2 (Propaganda Due), a secret Masonic lodge run from Arezzo by Italian businessman Licio Gelli, enrolled senior figures in Argentina's government and armed forces. Its membership lists, seized in Italy in March 1981, named navy commander and junta member Emilio Massera; Social Welfare Minister José López Rega, whose ministry funded the Triple A death squad; and Raúl Lastiri, interim president in 1973. Gelli in turn held an honorary diplomatic post at Argentina's embassy in Rome and was issued Argentine diplomatic passports, which Massera defended, saying Gelli had supported the junta 'in the struggle against subversion'. An Italian parliamentary inquiry, the Anselmi Commission, reported on the lodge in 1984.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Propaganda Due', 'Licio Gelli'; P2 membership lists seized March 1981; Anselmi Commission (1984)

channels.n: NATO's secret stay-behind network inside Italy: Brussels → Rome
channels.d: NATO's Clandestine Planning Committee and Allied Clandestine Committee, run from Brussels, coordinated Gladio, a secret armed 'stay-behind' network inside Italy's military intelligence service, SISMI. It was set up to resist a Soviet invasion, and parliament was not told it existed. Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti disclosed it to the Chamber of Deputies on 24 October 1990, the day after the last committee meeting under Belgian General Van Calster, and gave a list of 622 civilian members; he said 127 hidden arms caches had been dismantled. On 22 November 1990 the European Parliament called for all such networks to be investigated, and inquiries followed in Belgium and Switzerland.
channels.cite: Andreotti statement 24 Oct 1990; Wikipedia 'Operation Gladio'; European Parliament resolution 22 Nov 1990

channels.n: US-funded Counter-Guerrilla inside Turkey's army: Brussels → Ankara
channels.d: Turkey's branch of NATO's secret stay-behind networks was the Counter-Guerrilla, a unit hidden inside the army's Special Warfare Department and coordinated through NATO's Allied Clandestine Committee. It was paid for from outside the Turkish government: Prime Minister Bülent Ecevit, who revealed its existence in 1973, said he learned of it only when General Kemal Yamak asked him for money after US financing ended around 1973–74. Ecevit suspected the unit in the 1977 Taksim Square shooting, whose gunmen were never caught. Former prosecutor Emin Değer documented its ties to the Grey Wolves, an ultranationalist militia, whose links to state officials the 1996 Susurluk crash later exposed.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Operation Gladio', 'Grey Wolves (organization)'; Statements of PM Bülent Ecevit

channels.n: Stay-behind units inside Greece's army: Brussels → Athens
channels.d: Greece's part of NATO's secret stay-behind networks sat inside the Greek army as the LOK mountain raider units, with a branch called Operation Sheepskin, and was coordinated through NATO's Allied Clandestine Committee in Brussels. Like the other national networks, it was set up by NATO and Western intelligence services after 1945 to resist a Soviet invasion, without most parliaments knowing. The Greek defence minister said it operated until 1988. It came to light after Italy disclosed its own network, Gladio, in October 1990; a Belgian parliamentary inquiry in 1991 found the committee had coordinated networks in ten countries.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Operation Gladio'; Belgian parliamentary inquiry 1991

channels.n: Stay-behind networks inside Belgium, the Netherlands and Denmark
channels.d: NATO's Allied Clandestine Committee coordinated secret stay-behind networks inside the defence and security services of Belgium, the Netherlands and Denmark, unknown to their parliaments. Belgium's was run by a secretariat, SDRA XI, paid for with secret NATO money, with a military section under military intelligence and a civilian section under State Security; a Senate inquiry in 1991 found the committee coordinated networks in ten countries and criticised the refusal to name civilian members. In the Netherlands Prime Minister Ruud Lubbers told parliament in 1990 of a secret organisation inside the defence ministry; arms caches had been found near Rozendaal (1983) and Velp. Denmark's network was called Absalon.
channels.cite: Belgian parliamentary inquiry 1991; Wikipedia 'Operation Gladio'; Belgian Senate commission (Lallemand), 1991

channels.n: Unification Church ties to Japan's ruling party: Seoul → Tokyo
channels.d: The Unification Church, a religious movement founded in Seoul by Sun Myung Moon, built ties with lawmakers of Japan's governing Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) by supplying money, events and campaign volunteers; former prime minister Nobusuke Kishi co-founded its political arm. In September 2022, two months after former prime minister Shinzo Abe was killed, the LDP published a survey of its 379 members of parliament: 179 reported ties to the church, 29 had accepted donations and 17 had used its followers as campaign volunteers. Japan holds a large share of the church's membership. The Tokyo District Court ordered the church's Japanese corporation dissolved on 25 March 2025; the order was upheld in 2026.
channels.cite: Nippon.com / Jiji, 25 Mar 2025; LDP internal survey, 8 Sept 2022 (AP)

channels.n: Scientology agents inside US agencies: Saint Hill → Los Angeles → Washington
channels.d: The Church of Scientology's Guardian's Office, its intelligence and legal arm, headquartered at Saint Hill Manor in England with a US base in Los Angeles, placed members in US government jobs to copy files about the church, in a programme called Operation Snow White. Gerald Bennett Wolfe took a clerk-typist job at the Internal Revenue Service, the US tax agency, around 1974 and copied its files; others took documents from the Justice Department and a federal prosecutor's office. The FBI caught two operatives in a federal courthouse in 1976 and raided church offices on 8 July 1977. Eleven executives, including Mary Sue Hubbard, were convicted in 1979.
channels.cite: United States v. Hubbard; Wikipedia 'Operation Snow White'

channels.n: Scientology members inside Ontario police and law offices: Saint Hill → Toronto
channels.d: Operation Snow White, run by the Church of Scientology's Guardian's Office from Saint Hill Manor in England, extended to Canada. The Church of Scientology of Toronto placed members as staff inside the Ontario Provincial Police and the Ontario Ministry of the Attorney General, which runs prosecutions in the province, and also targeted the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. On 25 June 1992 the church itself was convicted of breach of the public trust, a crime of abusing a public position; seven members were convicted in all and the church was fined $250,000. The Court of Appeal for Ontario later rejected its appeal.
channels.cite: R. v. Church of Scientology of Toronto (1992); Court of Appeal for Ontario, 1997

channels.n: Hizb ut-Tahrir's alleged army coup plots: Jerusalem → Amman / Damascus
channels.d: Hizb ut-Tahrir, a pan-Islamist party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 that aims to restore a caliphate (a single Islamic state under one ruler), has tried to take power through members and recruits inside national armies. It was allegedly involved in failed coup attempts in Jordan and Syria in 1968–69 and in Egypt in 1974, and a 2004 Nixon Center report cited credible reports of members in coup plots in Jordan, Syria, Egypt, Tunisia and Iraq. These earlier plots rest on allegations. In Pakistan, a military court in 2012 convicted a serving brigadier and four majors of links to the group, which the army said had tried to recruit officers for a coup.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Hizb ut-Tahrir'; Nixon Center report 2004; Pakistan Army court martial, Aug 2012

channels.n: Trilateral Commission members staffed Carter's government: New York → Washington
channels.d: The Trilateral Commission, a private forum of business and political figures from North America, Western Europe and Japan, was founded in 1973 at banker David Rockefeller's insistence, with Zbigniew Brzezinski as organiser. Jimmy Carter and Walter Mondale were members before they took office as President and Vice-President in 1977, and other members followed them into the administration. In April 1980 the Christian Science Monitor counted 21 former members holding posts in it, including Brzezinski as National Security Adviser and Harold Brown as Defense Secretary. The count is a newspaper's; no inquiry has examined whether the commission shaped the administration's decisions.
channels.cite: Christian Science Monitor, 17 Apr 1980

channels.n: CFR wrote secret war planning for the State Department: New York → Washington
channels.d: The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a private New York foreign-policy club, wrote postwar planning papers for the US State Department in a confidential programme. From 1939 to 1945 its War and Peace Studies, paid for entirely by the Rockefeller Foundation, produced 682 memoranda, which the State Department classified and circulated among government departments; council members outside the project were not told it existed. Allen Dulles, later director of the CIA, led its security group. CFR members went on to hold about half of the top US foreign-policy posts from 1945 to 1972. The programme is described in the council's own history and in Shoup and Minter's Imperial Brain Trust (1977).
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Council on Foreign Relations'; Shoup and Minter, Imperial Brain Trust (1977)

channels.n: WEF Young Global Leaders who went on to lead governments
channels.d: The World Economic Forum (WEF), a Swiss foundation based in Cologny near Geneva and best known for its Davos meeting, works to shape government policy through cooperation between companies and states. Since 1992 it has picked rising politicians and business people, now under about 40, for a leadership network, today the Young Global Leaders, a five-year programme of meetings and courses. Alumni who later led governments include Justin Trudeau (Canada), Emmanuel Macron (France), Jacinda Ardern (New Zealand) and Sanna Marin (Finland); a 2021 paper by the German Bundestag's research service lists several of them. Membership is a WEF selection; no inquiry has found that the network directed their decisions.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Forum of Young Global Leaders'; Deutscher Bundestag, Wissenschaftliche Dienste, WD 1-3000-014/21 (2021)

channels.n: Mont Pelerin Society members in top economic posts
channels.d: The Mont Pelerin Society, a free-market society of economists and thinkers that works to spread free-market ideas into policy, has had members in the top economic posts of several governments. Friedrich Hayek founded it in 1947 at a meeting in the Swiss village of Mont Pèlerin; it is now headquartered at Texas Tech University in Lubbock, Texas. Members who held office include Ludwig Erhard, who joined in 1950 while West Germany's economics minister and used its meetings to test his plans, Luigi Einaudi (President of Italy), Václav Klaus (Czech finance minister, prime minister and president), Carlos Cáceres (Chilean finance minister) and Ranil Wickremesinghe (Sri Lankan prime minister). No inquiry has found that the society directed their decisions.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Mont Pelerin Society'; Wikipedia 'Mont Pelerin Society' (headquarters at Texas Tech University); Mont Pelerin Society Directory (2010)

channels.n: ALEC's Stand Your Ground model bill: Tallahassee → Arlington → ~30 states
channels.d: The American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC), based in Arlington, Virginia, brings corporate members and state legislators together to draft 'model bills', which the legislators then introduce in their own states as their own. After Florida passed its 'Stand Your Ground' law in 2005, allowing deadly force in self-defence without first retreating, ALEC adopted a model bill with the same wording, and similar laws spread to about 30 states with its support. In 2011 the Center for Media and Democracy and The Nation published about 850 ALEC model bills; about 1,000 ALEC-based bills were then introduced each year and roughly 20% enacted. After the 2012 killing of Trayvon Martin, more than 60 corporations and 34 legislators left ALEC.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'American Legislative Exchange Council'; Center for Media and Democracy, 'ALEC Exposed', 13 July 2011

channels.n: BCCI's secret control of First American: Luxembourg → London → Washington
channels.d: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), registered in Luxembourg and run from London and Karachi, secretly controlled First American Bankshares, Washington's largest bank, through nominee investors who held shares in their own names on its behalf, while US regulators were told BCCI was not involved. First American's chairman was Clark Clifford, a former US Defense Secretary, and its president was his law partner Robert Altman; the Kerry–Brown Senate report of 1992 found both closely involved with BCCI from 1978 to 1991. In July 1992 they were indicted for helping BCCI gain control of the bank. The state charges against Clifford were dismissed in 1993 because of his ill health, and Altman was acquitted.
channels.cite: Kerry–Brown report to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 1992; Indictments July 1992; New York Supreme Court dismissal, Nov 1993

channels.n: BCCI money behind Noriega's chosen president: London → Panama City
channels.d: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), run from London, handled the accounts of Manuel Noriega, Panama's military ruler, and on his instructions paid off the mortgage of Nicolás Ardito Barletta, Noriega's chosen presidential candidate, who became president of Panama in 1984. That put BCCI money behind the man Noriega placed at the head of the government. The US Senate's Kerry–Brown report of 1992 set this out; BCCI bankers Amjad Awan and Syed Hussain reportedly managed Noriega's accounts, and the bank was accused of laundering his money. A Luxembourg court ordered BCCI liquidated in July 1991.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'BCCI'; Kerry–Brown report, 'The BCCI Affair' (1992), ch. 5

channels.n: United Front reached UK MPs through Christine Lee: Beijing → London
channels.d: The United Front Work Department, a Chinese Communist Party department that builds influence over foreign politicians through overseas Chinese groups and individuals, reached into the UK Parliament through London solicitor Christine Lee, according to Britain's security service, MI5. In January 2022 MI5 sent MPs an interference alert saying Lee was suspected of political interference on the department's behalf. She had given more than £420,000 over five years to Labour MP Barry Gardiner. Neither was accused of a crime, and China denied the claims.
channels.cite: MI5 interference alert, Jan 2022; The Week, Jan 2022

channels.n: Chinese interference inside Canada's Parliament: Beijing → Toronto → Ottawa
channels.d: China's government has tried to reach inside Canada's Parliament. In 2023 Special Rapporteur David Johnston found 'irregularities' in Han Dong's 2019 Liberal nomination in Toronto's Don Valley North and a 'well-grounded suspicion' they were tied to China's Toronto consulate, though no evidence Dong knew; Canada's elections commissioner later found no breach of election law. In June 2024 Parliament's own intelligence committee, NSICOP, reported that some unnamed MPs and senators were 'witting' or 'semi-witting' participants in foreign interference, including taking disguised funds, and named China as a main perpetrator. The Hogue Commission found in January 2025 no evidence of 'traitors' in Parliament.
channels.cite: Federal Court of Canada 2022; Johnston report, May 2023; NSICOP special report, 3 June 2024; Hogue Commission, Jan 2025; Commissioner of Canada Elections, Aug 2025

channels.n: Hochul aide Linda Sun charged as China's agent: Beijing → New York
channels.d: Linda Sun, deputy chief of staff to New York Governor Kathy Hochul in 2021–22 after serving in Andrew Cuomo's administration, was charged on 3 September 2024 with secretly acting as an agent of China's government from inside the governor's office. Prosecutors allege she blocked contact between the office and Taiwan's representatives, steered messaging on Uyghurs, and worked with the Henan Association of Eastern America, a group tied to China's united front influence system, to arrange a Hochul visit to Henan. Her trial ended in a mistrial on 22 December 2025 when the jury deadlocked, and prosecutors said they would retry. Separately, the US indicted Liang Litang as an illegal agent in May 2023.
channels.cite: US Treasury sanctions 2021; US DOJ indictment 2023; United States v. Linda Sun and Chris Hu (E.D.N.Y.), mistrial Dec 2025

channels.n: Chinese-linked donor paid Senator Dastyari's bills: Beijing → Sydney / Canberra
channels.d: A Chinese company linked to political donor Huang Xiangmo paid $44,000 of Australian Labor senator Sam Dastyari's legal bills in 2014. Huang chaired the Australian Council for the Promotion of Peaceful Reunification of China, a peak body for groups linked to the United Front, the Chinese Communist Party's network for influence abroad. At a June 2016 press conference for Chinese media, with Huang present, Dastyari said China's borders were 'a matter for China', against Labor policy on the South China Sea, and in October 2016 he reportedly warned Huang his phone was probably tapped by Australian agencies. He lost his party posts in November 2017 and announced his resignation on 12 December 2017.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Sam Dastyari'; AAP (InDaily, 12 Dec 2017)

channels.n: Susurluk crash exposed Grey Wolves working with the state: Ankara → Susurluk
channels.d: The Grey Wolves, the militant youth wing of Turkey's Nationalist Movement Party, worked alongside Turkish police and politicians, and a car crash near Susurluk on 3 November 1996 showed it. In the car were Abdullah Çatlı, the group's second-in-command, wanted by Interpol for murder and drug trafficking, who carried a false passport and a gun licence signed by Interior Minister Mehmet Ağar; Hüseyin Kocadağ, deputy chief of the Istanbul police; and MP Sedat Bucak. Ağar resigned within days. A parliamentary inquiry reported in April 1997 that state bodies had used the Grey Wolves, and in 2001 a court sentenced Ibrahim Şahin and Korkut Eken to six years each.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Grey Wolves (organization)'; Susurluk inquiry report, April 1997; Istanbul court verdict 12 Feb 2001

channels.n: Black Hand officers used Serbia's army for the Sarajevo plot: Belgrade → Sarajevo
channels.d: The Black Hand, a secret society of Serbian army officers, used its members' posts inside the army to organise killings. Its leader, Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević ('Apis'), who had led the 1903 coup in which officers killed the king and queen, was made chief of the army's General Staff intelligence in 1913. Many scholars hold that he sanctioned the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand: three young Bosnian Serbs were recruited, trained and smuggled from Serbia into Bosnia, with the Black Hand supplying weapons, and the killing on 28 June 1914 helped set off the First World War. His role is disputed. In 1917 he was court-martialled for treason and shot.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Black Hand (Serbia)'; Salonika court-martial 1917; Encyclopaedia Britannica

channels.n: US Fellowship network's Ugandan chair and the anti-gay bill: Washington → Kampala
channels.d: The Fellowship (also called The Family), a Washington-based Christian network that builds private ties with lawmakers through prayer groups and national prayer breakfasts, has a Ugandan arm chaired by politician David Bahati. Journalist Jeff Sharlet reported that Bahati first floated his 2009 Anti-Homosexuality Bill, which proposed the death penalty, at the 2008 Uganda National Prayer Breakfast. Fellowship member Bob Hunter confirmed Bahati's link to the network to NPR; a Fellowship member denied that its associates were behind the bill. In 2023 the Fellowship paid for a US congressman's keynote at Uganda's breakfast. Bahati has been a state minister since 2021.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'The Fellowship (Christian organization)'; NPR, Dec 2009; Wikipedia 'David Bahati'

channels.n: Russian agent Maria Butina into US political circles: Moscow → Washington
channels.d: Maria Butina, working under Russian official Alexander Torshin, built back channels for Russia into Republican circles in the United States through the National Rifle Association. The National Prayer Breakfast, an event run by the Christian network the Fellowship and attended by the president, served as a meeting place: she helped arrange Russian attendance in February 2017, and a planned private meeting between Torshin and President Trump was cancelled after a national security aide flagged him. Butina pleaded guilty on 13 December 2018 to conspiring to act as an undeclared agent of a foreign government and was sentenced to 18 months. The FBI interviewed Fellowship organiser Doug Burleigh about her.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'The Fellowship (Christian organization)'; United States v. Maria Butina (D.D.C.), plea 13 Dec 2018, sentence 26 Apr 2019

channels.n: Moon's church bought into a Uruguayan bank that lent to its firms: Seoul → Montevideo
channels.d: The Unification Church, the Seoul-based religious movement led by Sun Myung Moon, took part-ownership of one of Uruguay's oldest banks during military rule, and the bank then lent heavily to the church's own businesses. In 1981 Moon's group bought 49% of Banco de Crédito; that year it also founded the daily Últimas Noticias, which declared itself 'fully identified' with the military government. Banco de Crédito closed in 2002. Uruguay's parliamentary commission on the banking system found it had taken excessive risk by lending about US$100 million to Moon-linked companies, out of about US$600 million in total loans.
channels.cite: El Observador, 1 September 2012; Uruguayan parliamentary investigative commission on the financial and banking system

channels.n: Chinese office paid Taiwan village chiefs' trips: Taizhou → Chiayi
channels.d: The Taiwan Affairs Office of Taizhou, a Chinese city government office, paid lodging and local travel for village and ward chiefs from Chiayi, who are elected local officials in Taiwan, on 2023 trips to Zhejiang organised by Lin Hsueh-feng, a former Kuomintang city council candidate. Prosecutors said Chinese officials on the trips urged the chiefs to vote for a particular party's candidate. On 28 May 2025 Chiayi District Court sentenced Lin to four years in prison under the Anti-Infiltration Act, a law against campaigning or political donations directed by hostile foreign forces. The ruling could be appealed.
channels.cite: Tribune India (CNA), 31 May 2025; Chiayi District Court, judgment of 28 May 2025

channels.n: CIA secretly funded and ran the Congress for Cultural Freedom
channels.d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly paid for and ran the Congress for Cultural Freedom, an anti-communist organisation of writers and intellectuals founded in West Berlin in 1950. The CIA's International Organizations Division funded its Paris secretariat, run by CIA officer Michael Josselson, which subsidised national committees in about 35 countries and more than 20 magazines, including Encounter in London, Preuves in Paris, Quadrant in Sydney and Transition in Kampala. The New York Times reported the CIA funding in April 1966, and in May 1967 former CIA official Thomas Braden admitted it in print. The Ford Foundation then took over funding until the body dissolved in 1979.
channels.cite: Saturday Evening Post (Braden), May 1967; New York Times, April 1966; CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence

channels.n: CIA money through the AFL's union committee into European unions
channels.d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly passed money through the Free Trade Union Committee of the American Federation of Labor (AFL), a US union federation, to steer unions and politics in Western Europe. The committee, run from New York by Jay Lovestone, sent funds to its Paris representative Irving Brown, who subsidised France's Force Ouvrière union from 1948, Italian unions around Italy's 1948 election, and anti-communist dockworker groups in ports such as Marseille. Historian Anthony Carew found in 1998 that the CIA channelled money this way for about 20 years; French journalist Frédéric Charpier puts the CIA's payments to Brown and Lovestone at about $1 million a year in 1951–54.
channels.cite: Carew, Labor History (1998); Frédéric Charpier, La CIA en France (2008)

channels.n: US-funded AIFLD trained Brazilian unionists who joined the 1964 coup
channels.d: The American Institute for Free Labor Development (AIFLD), set up in 1962 by the US union federation AFL-CIO with business and government partners, ran training institutes for union leaders in São Paulo and Recife paid for by contracts with USAID, the US government's aid agency. Its director, William Doherty Jr., later said its Brazilian trainees were 'intimately involved' in the 1964 coup that overthrew Brazil's government. US government money had therefore trained people who, by AIFLD's own account, took part in removing that government. The claim rests on Doherty's statement, as reported by historian Cliff Welch. AIFLD was merged into the American Center for International Labor Solidarity in the mid-1990s.
channels.cite: Welch, LARR

channels.n: CIA secretly ran Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty
places: National Committee for a Free Europe, New York
channels.d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly created and funded Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty, which presented themselves as private stations. CIA money passed through the National Committee for a Free Europe, a front organisation in New York organised by Allen Dulles, to stations in Munich that broadcast into Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary and the Soviet Union, and the CIA and State Department set their broad policy. In 1971 Senator Clifford Case introduced a bill to take their funding out of the CIA budget. CIA funding ended in 1971–72, and from 1974 Congress funded the stations openly through a Board for International Broadcasting.
channels.cite: Wikipedia RFE/RL; Case bill 1971; Board for International Broadcasting Act 1973

channels.n: Ford-funded Berkeley economists ran Suharto's economy
channels.d: The Ford Foundation, a large US private foundation, paid for economists from the University of Indonesia to take graduate degrees at the University of California, Berkeley from the late 1950s. After Suharto took power in 1966 he made them his economic team, later called the 'Berkeley Mafia': Widjojo Nitisastro headed the planning agency BAPPENAS from 1967 to 1983 and wrote Indonesia's Five-Year Development Plans, and Ali Wardhana was Finance Minister from 1968 to 1983. Their programme cut inflation and opened the country to foreign investors. The Ford Foundation describes its role in its own history, 'Celebrating Indonesia'.
channels.cite: Ford Foundation, 'Celebrating Indonesia'; Hill and Thee, Bulletin of Indonesian Economic Studies (2008)

channels.n: US-funded 'Chicago Boys' took Pinochet's economic posts
channels.d: A US government aid scheme, later taken over by the Ford Foundation, linked the University of Chicago's economics department with Santiago's Catholic University and paid for 126 Chilean students to train under it between 1955 and 1973. Known as the 'Chicago Boys', its graduates wrote 'El ladrillo' ('The Brick'), the plan General Pinochet's military government adopted as its economic programme in 1975, and then held its economic posts: Sergio de Castro was economy and then finance minister, and Miguel Kast ran the planning office, the labour ministry and, from 1982, the Central Bank. The programme is described in Milton and Rose Friedman's memoir Two Lucky People (1998).
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Chicago Boys'; Milton and Rose Friedman, Two Lucky People (1998)

channels.n: Rio 2016 bid paid IOC member Lamine Diack for votes: Rio → Dakar
channels.d: Brazil's Rio 2016 Olympic bid paid a member of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), the body whose members vote on which city hosts the Games, to buy votes. Rio state governor Sérgio Cabral testified in 2019 that he paid $2 million to Senegalese IOC member Lamine Diack, through businessman Arthur Soares, before the IOC chose Rio at its October 2009 session in Copenhagen. In November 2021 a federal court in Rio sentenced Carlos Nuzman, head of the Brazilian Olympic Committee and the bid, to 30 years and 11 months for corruption and other crimes; he remained free while appealing.
channels.cite: 7th Federal Criminal Court, Rio (2021); Cabral testimony, July 2019 (BBC); Agência Brasil, 26 Nov 2021

channels.n: Tobacco firms worked inside the WHO through consultants and partners
channels.d: Tobacco companies, including Philip Morris and BAT, ran a hidden campaign to weaken tobacco control at the World Health Organization (WHO), the UN health agency. They placed their own consultants in WHO posts, secretly paid 'independent' experts, and worked through their food subsidiaries, which offered partnerships to UN agencies, and through other UN bodies such as the FAO and the World Bank. A committee of experts chaired by Thomas Zeltner examined company documents released in US lawsuits and reported in July 2000 that the placements raised 'serious questions about whether the integrity of WHO decision-making has been compromised'. The report led into the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (2003).
channels.cite: Zeltner Committee report (2000)

channels.n: Milner placed his recruits in South Africa's colonial government: London → Transvaal
channels.d: Alfred Milner, Britain's High Commissioner in South Africa, brought young Oxford graduates from London from 1901 and placed them in the colonial governments of the Cape, the Transvaal and the Orange River Colony after the Boer War. The group, known as Milner's Kindergarten, then used those posts to push for union of the four colonies: Patrick Duncan was Transvaal Treasurer and Colonial Secretary, Lionel Curtis and Richard Feetham were town clerks of Johannesburg, and Robert Brand was secretary of the Intercolonial Council. The Union of South Africa came into being in 1910. Most of them returned to London in 1909–10 and renamed the group the Round Table; Duncan and Feetham stayed.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Milner's Kindergarten'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 4

channels.n: Milner network set up Chatham House and the CFR: London → New York
channels.d: Lionel Curtis, a member of Lord Milner's London-based network of imperialists, the Round Table, convened British and American peace-conference experts at the Hotel Majestic in Paris on 30 May 1919, where they proposed an Anglo-American institute. The British side founded Chatham House in London in 1920; during the Second World War its research service was moved into the Foreign Office (1943–46), so the institute's staff worked inside the ministry. The American side formed the Council on Foreign Relations in New York in 1921, which wrote 682 confidential memoranda for the State Department in 1939–45. Historian Carroll Quigley says Chatham House treated the CFR as its American branch.
channels.cite: Chatham House (2019); CFR centennial history (2021); Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 182–191; Wikipedia 'Chatham House'; Wikipedia 'Council on Foreign Relations'

channels.n: Gupta network steered South African state money to Dubai
channels.d: The Gupta brothers used their closeness to President Jacob Zuma to get South African ministers and heads of state companies to act for their businesses, a practice South Africans call 'state capture'. Money then left the country through Dubai. The leaked #GuptaLeaks emails showed funds from the Free State provincial government's Vrede dairy project were laundered through Dubai and paid for the family's 2013 wedding at Sun City, and a 2017 report by the South African Council of Churches and academics estimated about R40 billion moved to Dubai from state-company deals in 2011–17. The Zondo Commission found in 2022 that ministers and state-company heads acted corruptly for the family, who have lived in Dubai since 2016.
channels.cite: News24 #GuptaLeaks (2017); SACC report (2017), as summarised on Wikipedia; Zondo Commission (2022)

channels.n: Egypt and Qatar bribed Senator Menendez
channels.d: Egypt's government, working through New Jersey businessmen, paid US Senator Bob Menendez in cash, gold bars and other gifts while he chaired the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, which shapes US arms sales and aid, including to Egypt. A halal-meat monopoly that Egypt granted to businessman Wael Hana's company was used to channel the bribes. Prosecutors showed that Menendez passed sensitive US information to help Egypt and spoke up for Qatar to help a New Jersey developer win Qatari royal investment. A Manhattan federal jury convicted him on all counts on 16 July 2024, including acting as a foreign agent; he resigned and was sentenced to 11 years in January 2025.
channels.cite: US v. Menendez (S.D.N.Y.), verdict 16 July 2024; Sentence 29 Jan 2025; Wikipedia 'Bob Menendez'

channels.n: Azerbaijan paid PACE members ('caviar diplomacy'): Baku → Strasbourg
channels.d: Azerbaijan's government paid members of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), the Strasbourg body of national MPs that monitors elections and political prisoners, to win their support, a practice the European Stability Initiative named 'caviar diplomacy' in 2012. Italian Luca Volontè, leader of the Assembly's centre-right group, took €2.39 million routed through Azerbaijan-linked companies and, PACE's investigators found, played 'an important role in undermining' a report on Azerbaijan's political prisoners; a Milan court jailed him for corruption in 2021. The independent investigation body reported breaches by members from several countries in April 2018, and in 2021 the Bundestag lifted the immunity of two German members.
channels.cite: PACE Independent Investigation Body 2018; Court of Milan 2021; European Stability Initiative (2012); German Bundestag immunity decisions, 2021

channels.n: Azerbaijani Laundromat paid European politicians: Baku → Tallinn → London
channels.d: Azerbaijan's ruling circle moved about $2.9 billion in 2012–14 through four UK-registered shell companies with accounts at Danske Bank's Estonian branch in Tallinn, and part of it paid European politicians, including people who defended Azerbaijan in the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly. Almost half came from an account at the International Bank of Azerbaijan linked to the Aliyev family, which rules the country. Recipients included German MP Karin Strenz and Slovenian MP Zmago Jelinčič. The scheme came to light in September 2017, when the OCCRP journalists' network and partner newspapers published 16,000 leaked transactions.
channels.cite: OCCRP, September 2017

channels.n: Qatar and Morocco cash into the European Parliament: Doha / Rabat → Brussels
channels.d: Belgian prosecutors say Qatar and Morocco paid cash to people inside the European Parliament to favour them, through former Italian MEP Pier Antonio Panzeri and his Brussels non-profit, Fight Impunity. Police raided homes and offices on 9 December 2022, found bags of cash and arrested Greek MEP Eva Kaili, then one of the Parliament's 14 vice-presidents; the Parliament removed her from that post by 625 votes to 1. MEPs Marc Tarabella and Andrea Cozzolino were arrested in February 2023. Panzeri took a plea deal in January 2023, admitting his role; the others deny wrongdoing. In February 2026 the Brussels Court of Appeal ruled the investigation lawful, so the case continues.
channels.cite: Belgian Federal Prosecutor's Office; European Parliament vote 13 Dec 2022; Brussels Court of Appeal, Feb 2026

channels.n: Salvini aide sought secret Russian oil money for the Lega: Moscow → Milan
channels.d: Gianluca Savoini, a long-time aide of Lega leader Matteo Salvini and president of the Milan-based Lombardy–Russia cultural association, negotiated with Russian counterparts an oil deal meant to channel Russian money secretly to the Lega, then part of Italy's governing coalition. The talks took place at Moscow's Metropol hotel in October 2018 and were recorded; the recording was published in 2019. Milan prosecutors investigated Savoini and others for international corruption. In April 2023 a judge closed the case, finding the actions were 'unequivocally aimed' at illegal party financing but that the deal never got far enough to be a crime.
channels.cite: Milan judge's dismissal order, April 2023

channels.n: Medvedchuk network paid European politicians: Moscow → Prague → parliaments
channels.d: Viktor Medvedchuk, a pro-Kremlin Ukrainian politician exchanged to Russia in 2022, paid European politicians to carry Russian positions inside their parliaments. Czech intelligence exposed the Prague-based news site Voice of Europe in March 2024 as run for him and used to pass money to politicians, with Belgium as a hub for meetings and payments. Prosecutors in Munich are investigating AfD politician Petr Bystroň, now an MEP, for bribery; he denies it. In London, former MEP Nathan Gill was jailed for 10 years and 6 months in November 2025 for taking bribes in 2018–19 from Ukrainian MP Oleg Voloshyn, who passed on Medvedchuk's requests for statements in the European Parliament.
channels.cite: Czech Security Information Service 2024; Old Bailey 2025; Czech government sanctions decision, 27 March 2024; Munich Public Prosecutor's Office

channels.n: Kosovo and Moldova spy services seized Gülen-linked Turks for Ankara
channels.d: Turkey's government, which calls the movement of preacher Fethullah Gülen a terrorist group, had intelligence officers in Kosovo and Moldova seize Gülen-linked Turks and send them to Turkey outside the law. On 29 March 2018 Kosovo police and intelligence flew five teachers and a doctor to Turkey without telling Prime Minister Ramush Haradinaj, who then sacked the interior minister and the intelligence chief; in 2023 a Pristina court jailed former intelligence chief Driton Gashi for abuse of office. On 6 September 2018 Moldova's intelligence service sent seven Turkish teachers to Turkey; in 2019 the European Court of Human Rights ruled this an illegal transfer.
channels.cite: Basic Court of Pristina 2023; ECtHR Ozdil and Others v. Moldova 2019; Kosovo government dismissals, 30 March 2018

channels.n: Odebrecht paid officials in 12 countries for public works
channels.d: Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction group, paid presidents, ministers and officials in 12 countries in Latin America and Africa to win public works contracts, running the payments through an in-house bribery unit it called the Structured Operations Division. In its December 2016 plea agreement with US, Brazilian and Swiss authorities it admitted paying $788 million in bribes between 2001 and 2016. The payments included about $35 million to Peru's president Alejandro Toledo for the Interoceanic Highway contract and $13.5 million to Ecuador's vice-president. Courts have since convicted presidents and ministers; a Lima court sentenced Toledo to 20 years in October 2024.
channels.cite: US DOJ plea agreement, Dec 2016; Peru, National Superior Court of Specialized Criminal Justice, 21 Oct 2024

channels.n: Glencore bribed officials in five African states
channels.d: Glencore, a Swiss-based commodity trader that buys and sells oil and metals, paid government officials to win oil business and favourable treatment. The UK Serious Fraud Office, which prosecutes major fraud and bribery, found that Glencore's UK oil arm paid more than $28 million in bribes in Nigeria, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire and South Sudan in 2012–16. In June 2022 the subsidiary pleaded guilty to seven counts of bribery at Southwark Crown Court. A month earlier Glencore had pleaded guilty in the United States to bribery from 2007 to 2018 and agreed to pay over $1 billion, and it also agreed to pay the Democratic Republic of Congo $180 million.
channels.cite: UK SFO, Southwark Crown Court, June 2022; US DOJ plea, May 2022

channels.n: Universal Church bishops in Brazil's Congress, cabinet and Rio City Hall
channels.d: The Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (IURD), a neo-Pentecostal church founded in Rio de Janeiro in 1977 by Edir Macedo and run from the top, has put its own clergy into public office in Brazil. Its pastors founded the Republicanos party in 2005, whose president, Marcos Pereira, is a church bishop and has served as a federal minister. Bishop Marcelo Crivella, Macedo's nephew, was a senator (2003–16), Minister of Fishing (2012–14) and mayor of Rio de Janeiro (2017–20); police arrested him in December 2020 in an investigation into kickbacks in his administration. Abroad, Angola removed the church's Brazilian leadership in 2020.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Universal Church of the Kingdom of God'; Wikipedia 'Marcelo Crivella', 'Republicanos'

channels.n: CIA and BND secretly owned Crypto AG: Zug → Langley / Pullach
channels.d: The US CIA, based in Langley, and West Germany's BND, based in Pullach, secretly bought Crypto AG, a Swiss company in Zug that sold encryption machines to governments, in June 1970 for US$5.75 million. Owning it let them have the machines weakened and read the coded messages of customer governments in more than 120 countries, an operation called Thesaurus and later Rubicon. The BND left around 1993 and the CIA stayed owner until the firm was liquidated in 2018. The Washington Post, ZDF and SRF revealed the ownership on 11 February 2020, and a Swiss parliamentary inquiry that year found Swiss intelligence had known of it and benefited.
channels.cite: Washington Post/ZDF/SRF 2020; Swiss parliamentary oversight inquiry, Nov 2020

channels.n: Russian intelligence inside Wirecard and Austria's spy service via Marsalek
channels.d: Jan Marsalek, chief operating officer of the German payments company Wirecard until 2020, worked with Russian intelligence while he held that post, German investigators and the UK Crown Prosecution Service say, which put a Russian intelligence contact in the top management of one of Germany's largest listed companies. Wirecard collapsed in June 2020 after admitting that €1.9 billion did not exist, and Marsalek fled to Russia. From there he directed a Bulgarian spy cell in Britain, convicted at the Old Bailey in 2025, and received material from Austrian intelligence officer Egisto Ott, convicted in Vienna in 2026, so the network also reached inside Austria's intelligence service.
channels.cite: Old Bailey 2025; Vienna court 2026; Munich prosecutors; Bundestag Wirecard inquiry (2020–21)

channels.n: North Korean IT workers inside US firms: Pyongyang → US laptop farms
channels.d: North Korea's government places its programmers inside foreign companies as remote employees under stolen or false identities, and their wages fund its weapons programmes. US helpers run 'laptop farms', homes holding company laptops so that the workers, mostly based in China and Russia, appear to be working from the United States. Christina Chapman ran one in Arizona that put workers in more than 300 US companies and was sentenced in July 2025 to 102 months. Kejia Wang, who met a North Korean contact in Shenyang and Dandong in China, and Zhenxing Wang ran another in New Jersey that placed workers at more than 100 US firms; both were sentenced in April 2026.
channels.cite: US DOJ 2025–26; US District Court for D.C., sentence July 2025; US DOJ sentences April 2026

channels.n: Russian Laundromat used Moldovan judges to move billions
channels.d: A Russian money-laundering network used judges inside Moldova's courts to move an estimated $20–80 billion out of Russia in 2010–14. Russian companies 'guaranteed' fake debts, and Moldovan judges then ordered the debts paid into Moldindconbank, which gave the transfers legal cover; the money moved on through Latvian banks to shell companies worldwide, many registered in the UK. The scheme was exposed by OCCRP, a network of investigative journalists, and the Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta, and Moldovan prosecutors later charged judges who had approved the debts.
channels.cite: OCCRP and Novaya Gazeta, Global Laundromat; Moldovan prosecutors

channels.n: Mafias secretly owned Malta-licensed betting firms: Calabria / Palermo → Valletta
channels.d: Italian mafia groups, the Calabrian 'Ndrangheta and Sicily's Cosa Nostra, secretly owned or ran online betting companies licensed by the Malta Gaming Authority, hiding their ownership behind fiduciaries (people holding the shares on their behalf), and used them to collect bets in Italy and launder money, Italian investigations from 2015 found. Francesco Martiradonna, said to be the hidden owner of Centurionbet, was arrested in 2017, and in January 2018 Palermo's Operation 'Game Over' issued 26 arrest warrants, after which the Malta Gaming Authority suspended licences. Some executives were later acquitted of mafia ties. OCCRP's Daphne Project set out the pattern in May 2018.
channels.cite: OCCRP Daphne Project (2018); Malta Gaming Authority licence suspensions

channels.n: Gambian president's rosewood monopoly: Casamance → Banjul → China
channels.d: Westwood Company Ltd, the Gambian firm that held the exclusive licence to export rosewood, was co-founded by The Gambia's own president, Yahya Jammeh, with Swiss national Nicolae Bogdan Buzaianu, according to a 2019 complaint by the Swiss NGO TRIAL International; the president's office had awarded the licence to a company he part-owned. The rosewood was mostly logged in Senegal's Casamance region, trucked into The Gambia and shipped from Banjul. The Gambia exported about $163 million of rosewood to China in 2014–17, the Environmental Investigation Agency reported in 2020.
channels.cite: TRIAL International (2019); EIA 'Cashing in on Chaos' (2020)

channels.n: Dutch cocaine fugitive protected inside Sierra Leone's ruling circle
channels.d: Jos Leijdekkers ('Bolle Jos'), a Dutch fugitive sentenced in absentia in Rotterdam in 2024 to 24 years for smuggling over 7 tonnes of cocaine, has 'high-level protection' inside Sierra Leone's ruling circle, Reuters reported on 25 January 2025, citing three sources and video. Two sources said he is married to President Julius Maada Bio's daughter Agnes, and the footage shows him two rows behind the president at a New Year's Day mass. Dutch police had believed he was living in Turkey. Sierra Leone said it was investigating and dismissed its head of immigration; the government denies knowing where he is.
channels.cite: Reuters (January 2025); Rotterdam District Court (2024)

channels.n: Morgan, National City and Kuhn, Loeb bankers → Federal Reserve Board
places: New York (Morgan, National City, Kuhn, Loeb)
channels.d: Senior New York bankers secretly wrote the draft of the law that set up the US central bank, and one of them then sat on its board. In November 1910 Henry Davison of J.P. Morgan & Co., Frank Vanderlip of National City Bank and Paul Warburg of Kuhn, Loeb & Co. went with Senator Nelson Aldrich and Assistant Treasury Secretary A. Piatt Andrew to the Jekyll Island Club in Georgia, where they drafted the Aldrich Plan. It was published in 1911 without naming its authors, and the participants did not admit the meeting until the 1930s. The Federal Reserve Act followed in 1913, and in 1914 President Wilson appointed Warburg to the first Federal Reserve Board in Washington.
channels.cite: Federal Reserve History, 'The Meeting at Jekyll Island'; Wikipedia 'Paul Warburg'

channels.n: Goldman Sachs people into treasuries and central banks
channels.d: Former Goldman Sachs partners and staff have moved into the government posts that regulate banks and set economic policy. Robert Rubin and Henry Paulson went from the top of Goldman to US Treasury Secretary, and Paulson's 2008 rescue of the insurer AIG paid Goldman $12.9 billion; Gary Cohn became the White House's economic chief. Mario Draghi, a Goldman vice chairman in 2002–05, became Governor of the Bank of Italy, President of the European Central Bank, which from 2014 supervised the euro area's largest banks, and Italy's prime minister; Mario Monti, a Goldman adviser, also led Italy. Mark Carney ran the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England before leading Canada, and Jörg Kukies joined Germany's finance ministry.
channels.cite: Wikipedia biographies of Rubin, Paulson, Cohn, Draghi, Monti, Carney, Kukies

channels.n: Lazard men placed in Britain's wartime Washington posts (Quigley)
channels.d: Historian Carroll Quigley writes that Robert Brand, a managing director of the London bank Lazard Brothers and a leader of the Round Table, a private network of British officials and financiers, moved men from the bank into Britain's wartime posts in Washington. Adam Marris, who had got his Lazard job through Brand, joined the British Embassy in 1940 and returned to Lazard in 1946; Brand's nephew Thomas Brand became chief executive on the British side of the Combined Production and Resources Board. Brand himself headed the British Food Mission and was the Treasury's representative in Washington (1944–46). Quigley says the network was 'monopolizing' the wartime embassy; that is his account.
channels.cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment pp. 60, 80–81, 304; Wikipedia 'Robert Brand, 1st Baron Brand'

channels.n: Bribes for Mozambique's hidden 'tuna bond' loans: London → UAE → Maputo
channels.d: Credit Suisse bankers in London arranged secret state-guaranteed loans to three Mozambican state companies in 2013–14 for tuna fishing and maritime security projects with the shipbuilder Privinvest, and bribes reached both the Mozambican officials involved and the bankers. The guarantees were hidden from Mozambique's parliament and the IMF. The US Justice Department said at least $200 million went in bribes and kickbacks, with kickbacks to the bankers paid through UAE companies; Finance Minister Manuel Chang took $7 million and was convicted in New York in 2024. When the loans surfaced in 2016 the IMF and World Bank froze support. Credit Suisse pleaded guilty to wire fraud in 2021.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Tuna bonds'; US DOJ; US District Court (E.D.N.Y.), verdict Aug 2024; US DOJ plea agreement Oct 2021

channels.n: Rigged Crypto AG machines read by the CIA: Steinhausen → Langley → Tehran
channels.d: Crypto AG, a Swiss maker of cipher machines in Steinhausen, was secretly owned by the CIA and West Germany's BND, which had the machines deliberately weakened so that they could read the coded messages of the more than 120 governments that bought them. Iran was one customer; its arrest of Crypto AG salesman Hans Bühler in 1992 nearly exposed the operation. The BND co-owned the firm from 1970 to about 1993 and the CIA until it was liquidated in 2018. The Washington Post, ZDF and SRF revealed the ownership in February 2020, and a Swiss parliamentary inquiry confirmed it that year.
channels.cite: Swiss parliamentary inquiry 2020; Washington Post/ZDF/SRF, Feb 2020; Wikipedia 'Crypto AG'
